**Geometry of the regions.** The three side lines of $T$ cut $D$ into seven regions: $D_0=T$; three *edge regions*, each across one side and between the extensions of the other two sides; and three *vertex regions* $D_1,D_2,D_3$ (the vertical angle at each vertex, intersected with $D$). A point $Y\notin T$ forms a convex quadrilateral with the vertices exactly when it lies in an edge region, so $\Omega$ is the union of the three edge regions.

**Assume ($*$) fails**: $|\Omega|<|T|/500<\pi/500$.

*Short overhangs.* Let the line $X_2X_3$ meet the circle at $B$ beyond $X_3$. The triangle $X_1X_3B$ lies in the edge region across $X_1X_3$, so $X_1X_3B\subset\Omega$. It shares the apex $X_1$ with $T$ and its base $X_3B$ lies on the line of the base $X_2X_3$, so
$$\frac{X_3B}{X_2X_3}=\frac{|X_1X_3B|}{|T|}<\frac1{500}.$$
The same holds for all six "overhangs" from a vertex to the circle along a side line: each is less than $\frac1{500}$ of the corresponding side, hence less than $\frac{2}{500}=\frac1{250}$.

*Small vertex regions.* Look at $X_1$. Let the line $X_1X_2$ meet the circle at $P$ (beyond $X_1$) and $Q$ (beyond $X_2$), and the line $X_1X_3$ at $P'$ (beyond $X_1$) and $Q'$ (beyond $X_3$). The chords $PQ$ and $P'Q'$ cross at $X_1$, so on the circle the points alternate $P,P',Q,Q'$. The vertex region $D_1$ is bounded by $X_1P$, $X_1P'$ and the arc $\widehat{PP'}$ not containing $Q,Q'$; it is convex (intersection of two circular segments). We have $|PP'|\le X_1P+X_1P'<\frac{X_1X_2+X_1X_3}{500}$.

We claim this arc is the minor one. Otherwise $Q$ and $Q'$ lie on the minor arc between $P'$ and $P$ (in the order $P',Q,Q',P$), which is at most a semicircle; on such an arc chord length increases with arc length, so $|PQ|\le|PP'|$ and $|P'Q'|\le|PP'|$. But $|PQ|\ge X_1X_2$ and $|P'Q'|\ge X_1X_3$, giving $X_1X_2+X_1X_3\le2|PP'|<\frac{2}{500}(X_1X_2+X_1X_3)$, absurd.

So the arc is minor; every point of it is within $|PP'|<\frac1{125}$ of $P$, hence within $\frac1{250}+\frac1{125}=\frac3{250}$ of $X_1$. Since $D_1$ is convex, it lies in the disc of radius $\frac3{250}$ about $X_1$. The same holds at $X_2,X_3$, so
$$|D_1|+|D_2|+|D_3|<3\pi\left(\frac{3}{250}\right)^2 .$$

*Contradiction.* A triangle in the unit disc has area at most $\frac{3\sqrt3}4$ (the inscribed equilateral triangle is extremal). Therefore
$$\pi=|D|=|T|+|\Omega|+\sum_{i=1}^3|D_i|<\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}+\frac{\pi}{500}+\frac{27\pi}{62500}\approx1.299+0.0063+0.0014<\pi,$$
a contradiction. Hence ($*$) holds, and $P(C\text{ is a quadrilateral})>P(C\text{ is a triangle})$. ∎

solutions.title: Roots-of-unity filter
solutions.body:
**Answer: $4^{n-1}+2^{n-1}$.**

Expand $(a+b+c+d)^n$ as a sum over all words $x_1x_2\cdots x_n$ (one letter chosen from each factor). A word with $A$ letters $a$ and $B$ letters $b$ contributes to
$$\frac{(a+b+c+d)^n+(-a-b+c+d)^n+(-a+b+c+d)^n+(a-b+c+d)^n}{4}$$
its monomial with coefficient
$$\frac{1+(-1)^{A+B}+(-1)^A+(-1)^B}{4}=\frac{(1+(-1)^A)(1+(-1)^B)}{4}=\begin{cases}1&A,B\text{ even},\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
So substituting $a=b=c=d=1$ counts exactly the required words:
$$\frac{4^n+0^n+2^n+2^n}{4}=\frac{4^n+2^{n+1}}{4}=4^{n-1}+2^{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1).$$
Check $n=2$: $4+2=6$. ✓

solutions.title: Choose the positions of $a$ and $b$ first
solutions.body:
Let $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and let $S$ be the set of positions holding $a$ or $b$. Then $|S|$ must be even (sum of two even numbers). An $n$-element set ($n\ge1$) has $2^{n-1}$ even-size subsets.

* $S=\varnothing$: every position is $c$ or $d$, giving $2^n$ words.
* $|S|=k>0$ even: choose which positions of $S$ hold $a$ — an even-size subset of $S$, $2^{k-1}$ ways (then the number of $b$'s, $k-$even, is even automatically) — and fill $N\setminus S$ with $c$/$d$ in $2^{n-k}$ ways: $2^{n-1}$ words for each such $S$.

There are $2^{n-1}-1$ nonempty even $S$, so the total is
$$2^n+(2^{n-1}-1)2^{n-1}=4^{n-1}+2^{n-1}.$$
**Answer: $4^{n-1}+2^{n-1}$.**

prompt:
Let $A$ and $B$ be $n\times n$ real matrices such that
$$\operatorname{rk}(AB-BA+I)=1,$$
where $I$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. Prove that
$$\operatorname{trace}(ABAB)-\operatorname{trace}(A^2B^2)=\tfrac12 n(n-1).$$
($\operatorname{rk}(M)$ denotes the rank of $M$; $\operatorname{trace}(M)$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $M$.)
answer: With $X=AB-BA$: $\operatorname{tr}X^2=2\operatorname{tr}(ABAB)-2\operatorname{tr}(A^2B^2)$, and $X+I=vw^T$ with $w^Tv=\operatorname{tr}(X+I)=n$ gives $\operatorname{tr}X^2=n(n-1)$.

solutions.title: Write $X+I$ as $vw^T$
solutions.body:
Let $X=AB-BA$. Using $\operatorname{tr}(PQ)=\operatorname{tr}(QP)$:
$$\operatorname{tr}(X^2)=\operatorname{tr}(ABAB)-\operatorname{tr}(ABBA)-\operatorname{tr}(BAAB)+\operatorname{tr}(BABA)=2\operatorname{tr}(ABAB)-2\operatorname{tr}(A^2B^2),$$
since $\operatorname{tr}(ABBA)=\operatorname{tr}(A^2B^2)=\operatorname{tr}(BAAB)$ and $\operatorname{tr}(BABA)=\operatorname{tr}(ABAB)$. So we must show $\operatorname{tr}(X^2)=n(n-1)$.

A rank-one matrix is $X+I=vw^T$ for column vectors $v,w$. Then
$$X^2=(vw^T-I)^2=v(w^Tv)w^T-2vw^T+I=(w^Tv-2)\,vw^T+I .$$
Also $\operatorname{tr}X=\operatorname{tr}(AB)-\operatorname{tr}(BA)=0$, so $w^Tv=\operatorname{tr}(vw^T)=\operatorname{tr}(X+I)=n$. Hence
$$\operatorname{tr}(X^2)=(n-2)\operatorname{tr}(vw^T)+n=(n-2)n+n=n(n-1),$$
and $\operatorname{tr}(ABAB)-\operatorname{tr}(A^2B^2)=\frac12n(n-1)$. ∎

solutions.title: Eigenvalues
solutions.body:
As in the first solution it suffices to show $\operatorname{tr}(X^2)=n(n-1)$ for $X=AB-BA$, where $\operatorname{tr}X=0$.

$X+I$ has rank $1$, so its kernel has dimension $n-1$: the eigenvalue $0$ of $X+I$ has geometric, hence algebraic, multiplicity at least $n-1$. The remaining eigenvalue $\mu$ (counted with multiplicity, over $\mathbb C$) satisfies $\mu+0=\operatorname{tr}(X+I)=n$. So the eigenvalues of $X$ are $-1$ ($n-1$ times) and $n-1$. The eigenvalues of $X^2$ are their squares, so
$$\operatorname{tr}(X^2)=(n-1)\cdot1+(n-1)^2=n(n-1). \qquad ∎$$

prompt:
Let $d\ge2$ be an integer. Prove that there exists a constant $C(d)$ such that the following holds: For any convex polytope $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, which is symmetric about the origin, and any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, there exists a convex polytope $L\subset\mathbb R^d$ with at most $C(d)\,\varepsilon^{1-d}$ vertices such that
$$(1-\varepsilon)K\subseteq L\subseteq K.$$
(For a real $\alpha$, a set $T\subset\mathbb R^d$ with nonempty interior is a convex polytope with at most $\alpha$ vertices if $T$ is the convex hull of a set $X\subset\mathbb R^d$ of at most $\alpha$ points, i.e., $T=\{\sum_{x\in X}t_xx\mid t_x\ge0,\ \sum_{x\in X}t_x=1\}$. For a real $\lambda$, put $\lambda K=\{\lambda x\mid x\in K\}$. A set $T\subset\mathbb R^d$ is symmetric about the origin if $(-1)T=T$.)
answer: Take a maximal family of boundary points $p_i$ with $p_i+\frac\varepsilon2K$ having disjoint interiors and $L=\operatorname{conv}\{p_i\}$; volume counting gives $m\le3^d\varepsilon^{1-d}$, and a separating functional shows $(1-\varepsilon)K\subseteq L$. So $C(d)=3^d$ works.

solutions.title: A maximal packing of small copies
solutions.body:
We show $C(d)=3^d$ works. $K$ is convex, compact, symmetric, with nonempty interior. Two facts: $aK+bK=(a+b)K$ for $a,b\ge0$ (convexity), and for a linear functional $\ell\ne0$, $h=\max_K\ell>0$ and $|\ell(y)|\le h$ for $y\in K$ (symmetry).

**Construction.** Call a finite set $\{p_1,\dots,p_m\}\subset\partial K$ *admissible* if the sets $K_i=p_i+\frac\varepsilon2K$ have pairwise disjoint interiors.

*Size bound.* Let $\{p_i\}$ be admissible. Clearly $K_i\subset K+\frac\varepsilon2K=(1+\frac\varepsilon2)K$. Also $K_i$ does not meet the interior of $(1-\frac\varepsilon2)K$: if $z=p_i+\frac\varepsilon2k\in K_i$ and $z=ak'$ with $k,k'\in K$, $a\ge0$, then $p_i=ak'-\frac\varepsilon2k\in aK+\frac\varepsilon2K=(a+\frac\varepsilon2)K$ (using $-k\in K$), and since $p_i\in\partial K$ this forces $a+\frac\varepsilon2\ge1$. So the $K_i$ are $m$ sets with disjoint interiors, each of volume $(\frac\varepsilon2)^d\operatorname{vol}K$, inside $(1+\frac\varepsilon2)K\setminus\operatorname{int}(1-\frac\varepsilon2)K$:
$$m\left(\frac\varepsilon2\right)^d\le\left(1+\frac\varepsilon2\right)^d-\left(1-\frac\varepsilon2\right)^d .$$
The right side is a polynomial in $\varepsilon$ with nonnegative coefficients and no constant term, whose coefficients sum to $(\frac32)^d-(\frac12)^d$; as $\varepsilon<1$ it is at most $(\frac32)^d\varepsilon$. Hence
$$m\le\left(\tfrac32\right)^d\varepsilon\cdot\left(\tfrac2\varepsilon\right)^d=3^d\varepsilon^{1-d}.$$
In particular admissible sets have bounded size, so there is an admissible set $\{p_1,\dots,p_m\}$ that is **maximal** (no boundary point can be added). Let $L=\operatorname{conv}\{p_1,\dots,p_m\}$; it has at most $3^d\varepsilon^{1-d}$ vertices.

**$L\subseteq K$** by convexity of $K$.

**$(1-\varepsilon)K\subseteq L$.** Suppose $p\in(1-\varepsilon)K\setminus L$. Since $L$ is compact and convex, a hyperplane separates $p$ from $L$: there is a linear functional $\ell$ with $\ell(p)>\max_L\ell=\max_i\ell(p_i)$. Let $h=\max_K\ell>0$, attained at $x\in\partial K$. By maximality, $\{p_1,\dots,p_m,x\}$ is not admissible (if $x=p_i$ this is also true trivially), so $x+\frac\varepsilon2K$ and some $K_i$ have a common interior point $z$. Writing $z=x+\frac\varepsilon2k_1=p_i+\frac\varepsilon2k_2$ with $k_1,k_2\in K$:
$$\ell(p_i)+\frac\varepsilon2h\ \ge\ \ell(z)\ \ge\ h-\frac\varepsilon2h,$$
so $\ell(p_i)\ge(1-\varepsilon)h$. But $p\in(1-\varepsilon)K$ gives $\ell(p)\le(1-\varepsilon)h\le\ell(p_i)$, contradicting the choice of $\ell$. Hence $(1-\varepsilon)K\subseteq L$; in particular $L$ has nonempty interior. ∎

*Remark (normed-space language).* $K$ is the unit ball of a norm $\|\cdot\|$; the construction is a maximal $\varepsilon$-separated subset of the unit sphere, and the separation step is the Hahn–Banach theorem.

prompt: A polynomial $p$ with real coefficients satisfies the equation $p(x+1)-p(x)=x^{100}$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$. Prove that $p(1-t)\ge p(t)$ for $0\le t\le 1/2$.
answer: Normalise $p(0)=0$; then $p(1-x)=-p(x)$, and $p''=100\cdot99\,P_{98}$ relates it to the analogous polynomials of lower even degree, whose signs on $(0,\frac12)$ alternate; for $x^{100}$ the polynomial is negative there, so $p(1-t)-p(t)=-2p(t)\ge0$. (Equivalently: $p=\frac{B_{101}}{101}+c$ with Bernoulli polynomial $B_{101}$.)

solutions.title: Symmetry and convexity of the polynomials $P_n$
solutions.body:
Let $\Delta q(x)=q(x+1)-q(x)$. On polynomials, $\Delta$ lowers the degree by exactly one (for $\deg q=m\ge1$, the leading term of $\Delta q$ is $m c_m x^{m-1}$), its kernel is the constants, and it maps polynomials of degree $\le m+1$ onto those of degree $\le m$ (dimension count). Hence for each $n\ge1$ there is a unique polynomial $P_n$ with
$$\Delta P_n=x^n,\qquad P_n(0)=0,$$
and then $P_n(1)=P_n(0)+0^n=0$. Our $p$ equals $P_{100}+\text{const}$, so we must show $P_{100}(1-t)\ge P_{100}(t)$ on $[0,\frac12]$.

**Symmetry: $P_n(1-x)=(-1)^{n+1}P_n(x)$.** Let $S(x)=P_n(1-x)$. Then $\Delta S(x)=P_n(-x)-P_n(1-x)=-\Delta P_n(-x)=-(-x)^n=(-1)^{n+1}x^n$. So $S-(-1)^{n+1}P_n\in\ker\Delta$ is constant, and its value at $0$ is $P_n(1)-(-1)^{n+1}P_n(0)=0$. ✓

So $P_{100}(1-t)-P_{100}(t)=-2P_{100}(t)$, and it suffices to prove $P_{100}\le0$ on $[0,\frac12]$. Note also $P_{2k}(\frac12)=-P_{2k}(\frac12)$, so $P_{2k}(\frac12)=0$.

**Derivatives.** $\Delta(P_n')=(\Delta P_n)'=nx^{n-1}=\Delta(nP_{n-1})$, so $P_n'=nP_{n-1}+c_n$ for a constant $c_n$ ($n\ge2$). For odd $n=2k+1$, differentiating the symmetry $P_{2k+1}(1-x)=P_{2k+1}(x)$ gives $P_{2k+1}'(\frac12)=0$; with $P_{2k}(\frac12)=0$ this yields $c_{2k+1}=0$. Hence for $k\ge2$
$$P_{2k}''=2k\,P_{2k-1}'=2k(2k-1)P_{2k-2}.$$
Directly, $P_1=\frac{x^2-x}2$ (check: $\Delta P_1=\frac{2x+1-1}{2}=x$), so $P_2''=2P_1'=2x-1<0$ on $[0,\frac12)$.

**Signs.** $P_2$ is strictly concave on $[0,\frac12]$ and vanishes at both endpoints, so $P_2>0$ on $(0,\frac12)$. Then $P_4''=12P_2>0$: $P_4$ is strictly convex on $[0,\frac12]$ with zero endpoint values, so $P_4<0$ on $(0,\frac12)$. Inductively, $P_{2k}$ has sign $(-1)^{k+1}$ on $(0,\frac12)$. For $k=50$: $P_{100}<0$ on $(0,\frac12)$, and $P_{100}=0$ at $0,\frac12$.

Therefore $p(1-t)-p(t)=-2P_{100}(t)\ge0$ for $0\le t\le\frac12$. ∎

solutions.title: Maximum principle for a harmonic function
solutions.body:
Let $h(z)=p(1-\bar z)-p(z)$ for $z\in\mathbb C$. Since $p$ has real coefficients, $\overline{p(1-\bar z)}=p(1-z)$, so $\operatorname{Re}h(z)=\operatorname{Re}\big(p(1-z)-p(z)\big)$ is the real part of a polynomial, hence harmonic. On the real axis $h(t)=p(1-t)-p(t)$ is real, so we must show $\operatorname{Re}h\ge0$ on $[0,\frac12]$.

**Boundary values on the strip $0\le\operatorname{Re}z\le\frac12$.**
* $z=it$: $1-\bar z=1+it$, so $h(it)=p(1+it)-p(it)=(it)^{100}=t^{100}\ge0$.
* $z=\frac12+it$: $1-\bar z=z$, so $h=0$.
* Large $|t|$: as in the first solution, $\deg p=101$ with leading coefficient $\frac1{101}$. For fixed real $a$, $h(a+it)=p(1-a+it)-p(a+it)$ is a polynomial in $t$ and $a$ which vanishes identically at $a=\frac12$, so $h(a+it)=(1-2a)\big(t^{100}+Q(t,a)\big)$ where (comparing the top terms, $\frac{(1-a+it)^{101}-(a+it)^{101}}{101}=(1-2a)(it)^{100}+\dots$) $Q$ has degree $\le99$ in $t$ with coefficients polynomial in $a$. Hence $\operatorname{Re}h(a+it)\ge0$ for $a\in[0,\frac12]$ and $|t|\ge N$, $N$ large.

So $\operatorname{Re}h\ge0$ on the boundary of the rectangle $[0,\frac12]\times[-N,N]$. By the minimum principle for harmonic functions, $\operatorname{Re}h\ge0$ on the whole rectangle, in particular on $[0,\frac12]$: $p(1-t)\ge p(t)$. ∎

prompt:
Find all twice continuously differentiable functions $f:\mathbb R\to(0,+\infty)$ satisfying
$$f''(x)f(x)\ge2\big(f'(x)\big)^2\qquad\text{for all } x\in\mathbb R.$$
answer: Only the positive constants. $g=1/f$ satisfies $g''=\frac{2f'^2-ff''}{f^3}\le0$, and a positive concave function on $\mathbb R$ is constant.

solutions.title: $1/f$ is a positive concave function
solutions.body:
**Answer: exactly the positive constant functions.** Constants clearly work ($0\ge0$).

Let $g=1/f>0$. Then $g'=-f'/f^2$ and
$$g''=\frac{-f''f^2+2f(f')^2}{f^4}=\frac{2(f')^2-f''f}{f^3}\le0,$$
so $g$ is concave on $\mathbb R$.

**A positive concave function on $\mathbb R$ is constant.** Let $a<b$. For $u<a$ and $v>b$, concavity gives decreasing slopes:
$$\frac{g(a)-g(u)}{a-u}\ \ge\ \frac{g(b)-g(a)}{b-a}\ \ge\ \frac{g(v)-g(b)}{v-b}.$$
Since $g(u),g(v)>0$, the left side is $<\frac{g(a)}{a-u}$ and the right side is $>-\frac{g(b)}{v-b}$. Letting $u\to-\infty$ and $v\to+\infty$:
$$0\ \ge\ \frac{g(b)-g(a)}{b-a}\ \ge\ 0,$$
so $g(a)=g(b)$. Thus $g$, and hence $f=1/g$, is constant. ∎

solutions.title: $\arctan f$ is a bounded convex function
solutions.body:
Let $\phi=\arctan f$, which takes values in $(0,\frac\pi2)$. Then $\phi'=\frac{f'}{1+f^2}$ and
$$\phi''=\frac{f''(1+f^2)-2f(f')^2}{(1+f^2)^2}.$$
From the hypothesis, $f''\ge\frac{2(f')^2}{f}$, so $f''(1+f^2)\ge2(f')^2\left(\frac1f+f\right)\ge2f(f')^2$. Hence $\phi''\ge0$: $\phi$ is convex and bounded on $\mathbb R$.

A bounded convex function on $\mathbb R$ is constant: if $\phi'(x_0)\ne0$ for some $x_0$, say $\phi'(x_0)>0$, then $\phi(x)\ge\phi(x_0)+\phi'(x_0)(x-x_0)\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$ (tangent line bound), contradicting boundedness; similarly if $\phi'(x_0)<0$. So $\phi'\equiv0$ and $f=\tan\phi$ is constant.

**Answer: $f\equiv c$ for any constant $c>0$.** ∎

prompt: Find all prime numbers $p$ for which there exists a unique $a\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}$ such that $a^3-3a+1$ is divisible by $p$.
answer: Only $p=3$. If $a$ is a root of $f(x)=x^3-3x+1$ mod $p$, so are $a^2-2$ and $-a^2-a+2$; uniqueness forces $a^2-2=a$, i.e. $a\in\{-1,2\}$, and $f(-1)=f(2)=3$.

solutions.title: The map $x\mapsto x^2-2$ permutes the roots
solutions.body:
**Answer: $p=3$.**

Let $f(x)=x^3-3x+1$; we work in $\mathbb F_p$, where $\{1,\dots,p\}$ is a complete set of residues. (Over $\mathbb R$ the roots are $2\cos\frac{2\pi}9,2\cos\frac{4\pi}9,2\cos\frac{8\pi}9$, and $2\cos2t=(2\cos t)^2-2$ shows that $x\mapsto x^2-2$ permutes them; this motivates the following.)

Suppose $f(a)=0$ in $\mathbb F_p$. Then
$$g(x)=\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}=x^2+ax+(a^2-3)$$
and $f(x)=(x-a)g(x)$. Let $b=a^2-2$. A direct expansion gives
$$g(b)=(a^2-2)^2+a(a^2-2)+a^2-3=a^4+a^3-3a^2-2a+1=(a+1)f(a)=0 .$$
So $b$ is a root of $g$, and by Vieta the other root is $c=-a-b=-a^2-a+2$. Hence $a,b,c\in\mathbb F_p$ are all roots of $f$.

If $a$ is the **unique** root, then $b=a$: $a^2-a-2=(a-2)(a+1)=0$, so $a=2$ or $a=-1$. But $f(2)=3$ and $f(-1)=3$, so $0=f(a)=3$ in $\mathbb F_p$, i.e. $p=3$.

Conversely, for $p=3$: $f(1)=-1$, $f(2)=3$, $f(3)=19$; only $a=2$ gives a multiple of $3$. So $p=3$ is the only such prime. ∎

solutions.title: The discriminant is a square
solutions.body:
For $p=2$: $f(1)=-1$ and $f(2)=3$ are odd, so there is no root — not unique. For $p=3$: only $f(2)=3$ is divisible by 3 (as $f(1)=-1$, $f(3)=19$) — works.

Let $p>3$ and suppose $a\in\mathbb F_p$ is a root of $f$; let $b,c$ be the other two roots in a splitting field (at most $\mathbb F_{p^2}$, since $f=(x-a)g$ with $g$ quadratic over $\mathbb F_p$). The discriminant of $x^3+Px+Q$ is $-4P^3-27Q^2$; here $-4(-3)^3-27=81$, so
$$\big((a-b)(a-c)(b-c)\big)^2=81\ne0\quad(p>3),$$
and the roots are distinct. Now $(a-b)(a-c)=g(a)=f'(a)=3a^2-3\in\mathbb F_p^*$, so $(b-c)^2=\big(9/g(a)\big)^2$ and $b-c=\pm9/g(a)\in\mathbb F_p$. Also $b+c=-a\in\mathbb F_p$. As $p$ is odd, $b=\frac{(b+c)+(b-c)}2$ and $c$ lie in $\mathbb F_p$. So $f$ has three distinct roots in $\mathbb F_p$ whenever it has one — never exactly one.

**Answer: $p=3$.** ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a group and $n\ge2$ be an integer. Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be two subgroups of $G$ that satisfy
$$[G:H_1]=[G:H_2]=n\qquad\text{and}\qquad[G:(H_1\cap H_2)]=n(n-1).$$
Prove that $H_1$ and $H_2$ are conjugate in $G$.

(Here $[G:H]$ denotes the index of the subgroup $H$, i.e. the number of distinct left cosets $xH$ of $H$ in $G$. The subgroups $H_1$ and $H_2$ are conjugate if there exists an element $g\in G$ such that $g^{-1}H_1g=H_2$.)
answer: $H_1H_2$ is a union of $n-1$ left cosets of $H_2$ and of $n-1$ right cosets of $H_1$; so the complement $L=G\setminus H_1H_2$ is simultaneously a left coset $gH_2$ and a right coset $H_1g$, giving $g^{-1}H_1g=H_2$.

solutions.title: The complement of $H_1H_2$
solutions.body:
Let $K=H_1\cap H_2$. From $n(n-1)=[G:K]=[G:H_1][H_1:K]=n[H_1:K]$ we get $[H_1:K]=n-1$, and likewise $[H_2:K]=n-1$.

**$H_1H_2$ is a union of $n-1$ left cosets of $H_2$.** Write $H_1=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n-1}h_iK$. Since $K\subseteq H_2$, $KH_2=H_2$, so
$$H_1H_2=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n-1}h_iKH_2=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n-1}h_iH_2 .$$
These cosets are distinct: $h_iH_2=h_jH_2\iff h_i^{-1}h_j\in H_2$; since also $h_i^{-1}h_j\in H_1$, this means $h_i^{-1}h_j\in K$, i.e. $i=j$. So $H_1H_2$ consists of exactly $n-1$ of the $n$ left cosets of $H_2$, and its complement $L=G\setminus H_1H_2$ is a single left coset: $L=gH_2$ for any $g\in L$.

**Symmetrically**, writing $H_2=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{n-1}Kk_j$ (right cosets), $H_1H_2=\bigsqcup_jH_1k_j$ is a union of $n-1$ distinct right cosets of $H_1$. There are $n$ right cosets of $H_1$ (as many as left cosets, via $x\mapsto x^{-1}$), so $L$ is a single right coset: $L=H_1g$ for $g\in L$.

Hence for $g\in L$: $gH_2=L=H_1g$, i.e. $H_2=g^{-1}H_1g$. ∎

solutions.title: Group actions on coset spaces
solutions.body:
Let $X=G/H_1$ and $Y=G/H_2$ (left cosets), $|X|=|Y|=n$, with $G$ acting by left multiplication; let $x_0=H_1$, $y_0=H_2$. $G$ acts on $X\times Y$ coordinatewise. The stabiliser of $(x_0,y_0)$ is $H_1\cap H_2$, so by the orbit–stabiliser theorem its orbit $Z$ has $n(n-1)$ elements, and $W=(X\times Y)\setminus Z$ has $n$ elements. Both $Z$ and $W$ are $G$-invariant.

For $x\in X$ let $Z_x=\{y:(x,y)\in Z\}$. An element $g$ maps $Z_x$ bijectively onto $Z_{gx}$, and $G$ is transitive on $X$, so all $|Z_x|$ are equal, hence equal to $n(n-1)/n=n-1$. Similarly every "column" $\{x:(x,y)\in Z\}$ has $n-1$ elements. So $W$ meets every row and every column in exactly one point: $W$ is the graph of a bijection $\varphi:X\to Y$. Since $W$ is $G$-invariant, $(gx,g\varphi(x))\in W$, i.e. $\varphi(gx)=g\varphi(x)$.

Thus $\varphi$ is a $G$-equivariant bijection, so stabilisers correspond: $\operatorname{Stab}(x_0)=\operatorname{Stab}(\varphi(x_0))$. Writing $\varphi(x_0)=gH_2$, this reads $H_1=gH_2g^{-1}$, i.e. $g^{-1}H_1g=H_2$. ∎

*Remark.* The situation occurs for every $n\ge2$: $G=S_n$ and $H_1,H_2$ the stabilisers of two different points.

prompt:
Compute
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\log\log n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk\log k .$$
(Here $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm.)

solutions.title: Frullani integral
solutions.body:
**Answer: $1$.**

**Integral representation.** For $k\ge1$, Frullani's integral gives $\log k=\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-x}-e^{-kx}}{x}\,dx$. Since $\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^k\binom nk=-1$ and $\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^k\binom nke^{-kx}=(1-e^{-x})^n-1$,
$$A_n:=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^k\binom nk\log k=\int_0^\infty\frac{1-e^{-x}-(1-e^{-x})^n}{x}\,dx .$$
With $y=1-e^{-x}\in[0,1)$ the numerator is $y-y^n\ge0$.

**Tail.** By Bernoulli, $(1-e^{-x})^n\ge1-ne^{-x}$, so the numerator is $\le ne^{-x}$. Choose $M$ with $Me^M=n$ ($M\to\infty$). Then
$$0\le\int_M^\infty\frac{1-e^{-x}-(1-e^{-x})^n}{x}dx\le\frac nM\int_M^\infty e^{-x}dx=\frac{ne^{-M}}M=1 .$$

**Main part.** For $0\le x\le M$, $e^{-x}\ge e^{-M}=M/n$, so
$$(1-e^{-x})^{n-1}\le e^{-(n-1)e^{-x}}\le e^{-(n-1)M/n}=:\delta_n\to0 .$$
Writing the numerator as $(1-e^{-x})\big(1-(1-e^{-x})^{n-1}\big)$, we get
$$(1-\delta_n)I(M)\le\int_0^M\frac{1-e^{-x}-(1-e^{-x})^n}{x}dx\le I(M),\qquad I(M)=\int_0^M\frac{1-e^{-x}}x\,dx .$$
And $I(M)=\int_0^1\frac{1-e^{-x}}xdx+\int_1^M\frac{dx}x-\int_1^M\frac{e^{-x}}xdx=\log M+O(1)$.

**Size of $M$.** $M+\log M=\log n$, so $\log n-\log\log n\le M\le\log n$ for large $n$, and $\log M=\log\log n+o(1)$.

Altogether $A_n=(1+o(1))\log\log n+O(1)$, so
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{A_n}{\log\log n}=1 .$$

solutions.title: Finite differences of $1/x$
solutions.body:
**Two identities.** Partial fractions give
$$\sum_{j=0}^m(-1)^j\binom mj\frac1{x+j}=\frac{m!}{x(x+1)\cdots(x+m)},\tag{1}$$
(the residue at $x=-j$ of the right side is $\frac{m!}{\prod_{i\ne j}(i-j)}=(-1)^j\binom mj$). And by Pascal's rule (telescoping),
$$\sum_{k=j+1}^n(-1)^k\binom nk=(-1)^{j+1}\binom{n-1}j .\tag{2}$$

**Rewrite the sum.** $\log k=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}I_j$ with $I_j=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{x+j}=\log\frac{j+1}j$. Exchanging sums and using (2), then (1) with $m=n-1$:
$$S_n:=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^k\binom nk\log k=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(-1)^{j+1}\binom{n-1}jI_j=\int_0^1\left(\frac1x-\frac{(n-1)!}{x(x+1)\cdots(x+n-1)}\right)dx$$
$$=\int_0^1\frac{1}{x}\left(1-\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\Big(1+\frac xj\Big)^{-1}\right)dx .$$

**Estimate the product.** For $0<y\le1$: $e^{-y}\le\frac1{1+y}\le e^{y^2-y}$ (the right inequality from $e^{y^2-y}\ge1+y^2-y=\frac{1+y^3}{1+y}$). With $y=x/j$, $H=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac1j$ and $x^2\sum\frac1{j^2}\le2x$ for $x\in[0,1]$:
$$e^{-Hx}\le\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\Big(1+\frac xj\Big)^{-1}\le e^{-(H-2)x}.$$
Hence
$$\int_0^1\frac{1-e^{-(H-2)x}}{x}dx\le S_n\le\int_0^1\frac{1-e^{-Hx}}xdx .$$
For $c\to\infty$, $\int_0^1\frac{1-e^{-cx}}xdx=\int_0^c\frac{1-e^{-t}}tdt=\log c+O(1)$. Since $H=\log n+O(1)$, both bounds are $\log\log n+O(1)$, so $S_n=\log\log n+O(1)$ and the limit is
$$1 .$$

prompt:
Let $A$ be a real $n\times n$ matrix such that $A^3=0$.

(a) Prove that there is a unique real $n\times n$ matrix $X$ that satisfies the equation
$$X+AX+XA^2=A.$$
(b) Express $X$ in terms of $A$.
answer: $X=A-A^2$ (multiplying the equation by powers of $A$ on the left and right forces $XA^2=0$, $A^2X=0$, $AX=A^2$; then check $A-A^2$ works).

solutions.title: Multiply by powers of $A$
solutions.body:
Write $(E)$ for the equation $X+AX+XA^2=A$ and use $A^3=A^4=\dots=0$ throughout.

**Uniqueness.** Suppose $X$ satisfies $(E)$.

* Multiply $(E)$ by $A^2$ on both sides: $A^2XA^2+A^3XA^2+A^2XA^4=A^5$, i.e. $A^2XA^2=0$.
* Multiply $(E)$ by $A$ on the left and $A^2$ on the right: $AXA^2+A^2XA^2+AXA^4=A^4$, i.e. $AXA^2+A^2XA^2=0$, so $AXA^2=0$.
* Multiply $(E)$ by $A^2$ on the right: $XA^2+AXA^2+XA^4=A^3$, i.e. $XA^2+AXA^2=0$, so $XA^2=0$.

Hence $(E)$ reduces to $X+AX=A$. Multiplying this on the left by $A^2$ gives $A^2X+A^3X=A^3$, so $A^2X=0$; multiplying it on the left by $A$ gives $AX+A^2X=A^2$, so $AX=A^2$. Therefore
$$X=A-AX=A-A^2 .$$
So no matrix other than $A-A^2$ can satisfy $(E)$.

**Existence.** The steps above cannot simply be reversed, so we check directly: for $X=A-A^2$,
$$X+AX+XA^2=(A-A^2)+(A^2-A^3)+(A^3-A^4)=A-A^4=A .$$

Hence the equation has the unique solution
$$X=A-A^2 .$$
∎

solutions.title: A nilpotent linear operator
solutions.body:
**Existence and uniqueness at once.** Consider the linear map $L$ on the space $M_n(\mathbb R)$ of real $n\times n$ matrices given by
$$L(X)=X+AX+XA^2=(\mathrm{Id}+N)(X),\qquad N(X)=AX+XA^2 .$$
Write $N=\ell+r$ with $\ell(X)=AX$ and $r(X)=XA^2$. These two maps commute ($\ell r(X)=AXA^2=r\ell(X)$), and both are nilpotent: $\ell^3(X)=A^3X=0$, $r^2(X)=XA^4=0$. By the binomial theorem for commuting maps,
$$N^4=\sum_{j=0}^{4}\binom4j\ell^{j}r^{4-j}=0,$$
since each term has $j\ge3$ or $4-j\ge2$. So $N$ is nilpotent and $L=\mathrm{Id}+N$ is invertible, with inverse $\mathrm{Id}-N+N^2-N^3$. Hence $L(X)=A$ has exactly one solution.

**Finding it.** Since $I+A$ is invertible with inverse $B=I-A+A^2$ (indeed $(I+A)(I-A+A^2)=I+A^3=I$), the equation $(I+A)X+XA^2=A$ is equivalent to
$$X+BXA^2=BA .$$
Multiplying on the right by $A^2$ gives $XA^2+BXA^4=BA^3$, i.e. $XA^2=0$, so $X=BA=A-A^2+A^3=A-A^2$. (Conversely $X=BA$ satisfies $XA^2=BA^3=0$ and therefore the equation.)

**Answer:** the unique solution is $X=A-A^2$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ and $k$ be fixed positive integers, and let $a$ be an arbitrary non-negative integer. Choose a random $k$-element subset $X$ of $\{1,2,\dots,k+a\}$ uniformly (i.e., all $k$-element subsets are chosen with the same probability) and, independently of $X$, choose a random $n$-element subset $Y$ of $\{1,\dots,k+n+a\}$ uniformly.

Prove that the probability
$$P\big(\min(Y)>\max(X)\big)$$
does not depend on $a$.
answer: The probability equals $1\big/\binom{n+k}{k}$: the favourable pairs $(X,Y)$ correspond bijectively to the $(n+k)$-subsets $X\cup Y$ of $\{1,\dots,n+k+a\}$.

solutions.title: Count the favourable pairs
solutions.body:
Let $N=n+k+a$. All $\binom{k+a}{k}\binom{N}{n}$ pairs $(X,Y)$ are equally likely.

**Favourable pairs $\leftrightarrow$ $(n+k)$-subsets.** If $\min Y>\max X$, then $U=X\cup Y$ is an $(n+k)$-element subset of $\{1,\dots,N\}$, and $X$ consists of the $k$ smallest elements of $U$, $Y$ of the $n$ largest. Conversely, let $U\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}$ be any set of $n+k$ elements, let $X$ be its $k$ smallest and $Y$ its $n$ largest elements. Then $\min Y>\max X$, $|Y|=n$, and $X\subseteq\{1,\dots,k+a\}$: indeed the largest element of $X$ has the $n$ elements of $Y$ above it, all at most $N$, so it is at most $N-n=k+a$. So $(X,Y)$ is an admissible favourable pair, and the two maps are inverse to each other. Hence there are exactly $\binom{N}{n+k}$ favourable pairs.

**The probability.**
$$P=\frac{\binom{N}{n+k}}{\binom{k+a}{k}\binom{N}{n}}
=\frac{N!}{(n+k)!\,a!}\cdot\frac{k!\,a!}{(k+a)!}\cdot\frac{n!\,(k+a)!}{N!}
=\frac{n!\,k!}{(n+k)!}=\frac{1}{\binom{n+k}{k}} ,$$
which does not depend on $a$. ∎

solutions.title: Relabel and condition
solutions.body:
Let $N=n+k+a$. Given $Y$, let $f$ be the increasing bijection from $\{1,\dots,k+a\}$ onto the complement $\{1,\dots,N\}\setminus Y$ (which has $k+a$ elements).

**Claim:** $\min Y>\max X\iff \min Y>\max f(X)$. Let $y_0=\min Y$. The numbers $1,\dots,y_0-1$ all lie in the complement of $Y$ and are its smallest elements, so $f(x)=x$ for $x\le y_0-1$, while $f(x)>y_0$ for $x\ge y_0$ (as $f(x)\ge x$ and $f(x)\notin Y$). Hence $X\subseteq\{1,\dots,y_0-1\}$ iff $f(X)\subseteq\{1,\dots,y_0-1\}$.

Now put $Z_n=Y$, $Z_k=f(X)$ and $Z_a=f(\{1,\dots,k+a\}\setminus X)$. Since $Y$ is uniform and, given $Y$, $X$ is uniform and independent of $Y$, the set $f(X)$ is a uniform $k$-subset of the complement of $Y$. Hence $(Z_n,Z_k,Z_a)$ is a uniformly random ordered partition of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ into blocks of sizes $n,k,a$.

Condition on $Z_a$. Then $Z_n\cup Z_k$ is a fixed set of $n+k$ elements, and $Z_k$ is a uniformly random $k$-subset of it. The event $\min Z_n>\max Z_k$ means that $Z_k$ is exactly the set of the $k$ smallest of these $n+k$ elements, which has conditional probability $1/\binom{n+k}{k}$, whatever $Z_a$ is. Averaging over $Z_a$,
$$P\big(\min Y>\max X\big)=\frac{1}{\binom{n+k}{k}},$$
independent of $a$. ∎

prompt:
We say that a positive real number $d$ is *good* if there exists an infinite sequence $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots\in(0,d)$ such that for each $n$, the points $a_1,\dots,a_n$ partition the interval $[0,d]$ into segments of length at most $1/n$ each. Find
$$\sup\{d\mid d\text{ is good}\}.$$
answer: ln(2)

solutions.title: Intact segments give the bound; halving integrals give the construction
solutions.body:
**Answer: $\ln 2$.**

**Upper bound.** Let $d$ be good with witness sequence $(a_i)$, and fix $n$. The points $a_1,\dots,a_n$ cut $[0,d]$ into $n+1$ segments; let their lengths be $\ell_1\le\ell_2\le\dots\le\ell_{n+1}$.

Fix $k\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$. After adding the $k$ further points $a_{n+1},\dots,a_{n+k}$, at most $k$ of these $n+1$ segments have been cut, so at least $n+1-k$ of them are still segments of the partition by $a_1,\dots,a_{n+k}$, hence have length at most $\frac1{n+k}$. Thus at least $n+1-k$ of the numbers $\ell_j$ are $\le\frac1{n+k}$, i.e. $\ell_{n+1-k}\le\frac1{n+k}$. Summing over $k=0,\dots,n$:
$$d=\ell_1+\dots+\ell_{n+1}\le \frac1n+\frac1{n+1}+\dots+\frac1{2n}.$$
Since $\frac1j\le\int_{j-1}^{j}\frac{dx}{x}$, the right side is at most $\frac1n+\int_n^{2n}\frac{dx}x=\frac1n+\ln2$. Letting $n\to\infty$ gives $d\le\ln 2$.

**$\ln 2$ is good.** Put $I_m=\ln\frac{m+1}{m}=\int_m^{m+1}\frac{dx}{x}$ for $m\ge1$. Note
$$I_m<\frac1m\qquad\text{and}\qquad I_{2m}+I_{2m+1}=\ln\frac{2m+1}{2m}+\ln\frac{2m+2}{2m+1}=\ln\frac{m+1}{m}=I_m .$$
We build the points so that **after $n-1$ points the $n$ segments have lengths $I_n,I_{n+1},\dots,I_{2n-1}$** (in some order). For $n=1$ there are no points and the single segment $[0,\ln2]$ has length $\ln 2=I_1$. Given the statement for $n$, place $a_n$ inside the segment of length $I_n$, splitting it into pieces of lengths $I_{2n}$ and $I_{2n+1}$. The new lengths are $I_{n+1},\dots,I_{2n-1},I_{2n},I_{2n+1}$, as required for $n+1$. Each new point lies strictly inside a segment, so all $a_n\in(0,\ln 2)$.

Check the condition: after $n$ points the segments have lengths $I_{n+1},\dots,I_{2n+1}$, the largest being $I_{n+1}<\frac1{n+1}<\frac1n$. So $\ln2$ is good. (The first points are $a_1=\ln\frac32$, then $\ln\frac54$, and so on.)

Hence
$$\sup\{d\mid d\text{ is good}\}=\ln 2 .$$
∎

prompt:
Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a function. Suppose that for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a function $g:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ such that for every pair $(x,y)$ of real numbers,
$$\text{if}\quad |x-y|<\min\{g(x),g(y)\},\quad\text{then}\quad |f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon .$$
Prove that $f$ is the pointwise limit of a sequence of continuous $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ functions, i.e., there is a sequence $h_1,h_2,\dots$ of continuous $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ functions such that $\lim_{n\to\infty}h_n(x)=f(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb R$.
answer: For each $n$ cover $\mathbb R$ by the intervals of radius $\delta_n(x)=\min\{\frac1n,g_1(x),\dots,g_n(x)\}$ around the points $x$, take a locally finite subcover and a subordinate partition of unity, and let $h_n=\sum_U\varphi_U\,f(c_U)$. Then $h_n(x)$ is an average of values $f(c)$ with $|x-c|<\min\{g_m(x),g_m(c)\}$ once $n$ is large.

solutions.title: Partition of unity on a locally finite cover
solutions.body:
For $m=1,2,\dots$ let $g_m$ be a function given by the hypothesis for $\varepsilon=\frac1m$. For $n\ge1$ and $x\in\mathbb R$ put
$$\delta_n(x)=\min\Big\{\tfrac1n,\,g_1(x),\,g_2(x),\dots,g_n(x)\Big\}>0 .$$
Then for $m\le n$: if $|x-y|<\min\{\delta_n(x),\delta_n(y)\}$, then $|x-y|<\min\{g_m(x),g_m(y)\}$ and so $|f(x)-f(y)|<\frac1m$.

**Step 1: a locally finite cover.** Fix $n$. For $c\in\mathbb R$ let $U_c=(c-\delta_n(c),\,c+\delta_n(c))$. For every integer $j$ the compact interval $[j,j+1]$ is covered by the open intervals $U_c$, so finitely many of them, say the family $\mathcal F_j$, cover it. Let $\mathcal F=\bigcup_{j\in\mathbb Z}\mathcal F_j$. It covers $\mathbb R$, and it is locally finite: every interval of $\mathcal F_j$ meets $[j,j+1]$ and has length $\le\frac2n\le2$, so a bounded set meets intervals from only finitely many $\mathcal F_j$, each of which is finite. For each $U\in\mathcal F$ fix its centre $c_U$ and radius $r_U=\delta_n(c_U)$.

**Step 2: a partition of unity.** For $U\in\mathcal F$ let $\psi_U(x)=\max\{0,\,r_U-|x-c_U|\}$; it is continuous, positive exactly on $U$ and zero outside $U$. By local finiteness, near any point only finitely many $\psi_U$ are nonzero, so $\Psi=\sum_{U\in\mathcal F}\psi_U$ is continuous, and $\Psi>0$ everywhere because $\mathcal F$ covers $\mathbb R$. Define
$$h_n(x)=\sum_{U\in\mathcal F}\frac{\psi_U(x)}{\Psi(x)}\,f(c_U).$$
Again the sum is locally finite, so $h_n$ is continuous. For each $x$, $h_n(x)$ is a convex combination of the values $f(c_U)$ over those $U\in\mathcal F$ with $x\in U$, i.e. with $|x-c_U|<\delta_n(c_U)$.

**Step 3: pointwise convergence.** Fix $x\in\mathbb R$ and $m\ge1$, and let $n$ be any integer with $n\ge m$ and $\frac1n<\delta_m(x)$. Take $U\in\mathcal F$ (built for this $n$) containing $x$, with centre $c=c_U$. Then
$$|x-c|<\delta_n(c)\le g_m(c)\quad(\text{since }n\ge m),\qquad |x-c|<\delta_n(c)\le\tfrac1n<\delta_m(x)\le g_m(x).$$
So $|x-c|<\min\{g_m(x),g_m(c)\}$ and therefore $|f(x)-f(c)|<\frac1m$. As $h_n(x)$ is a convex combination of such values $f(c)$,
$$|h_n(x)-f(x)|<\frac1m .$$
This holds for all sufficiently large $n$, for every $m$; hence $h_n(x)\to f(x)$. Since $x$ was arbitrary, $f$ is the pointwise limit of the continuous functions $h_n$. ∎

*Remark.* Equivalently one can show that all sets $\{f\ge c\}$ and $\{f\le c\}$ are $G_\delta$ and invoke Lebesgue's characterisation of Baire class 1 functions; the construction above avoids that theorem.

prompt:
Let $A$ be a real $n\times n$ matrix and suppose that for every positive integer $m$ there exists a real symmetric matrix $B$ such that
$$2021B=A^m+B^2 .$$
Prove that $|\det A|\le1$.
answer: $m=1$ shows $A=2021B-B^2$ is symmetric, so its eigenvalues are real; for even $m$, $\frac{2021^2}{4}I-A^m=(B-\frac{2021}2I)^2$ is positive semidefinite, so $\lambda^m\le\frac{2021^2}4$ for every eigenvalue $\lambda$, forcing $|\lambda|\le1$.

solutions.title: Eigenvalues of a quadratic in a symmetric matrix
solutions.body:
Let $B_m$ be a real symmetric matrix with $2021B_m=A^m+B_m^2$, and put $h(t)=2021t-t^2$, so $A^m=h(B_m)$.

**$A$ is symmetric.** For $m=1$, $A=2021B_1-B_1^2$ is a polynomial in a symmetric matrix, hence symmetric. So $A$ is orthogonally diagonalisable with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$, and $\det A=\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n$.

**Each $|\lambda_i|\le1$.** Fix $m$. Since $B_m$ is real symmetric, $B_m=QDQ^T$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $D$ diagonal with real entries $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n$; then $A^m=h(B_m)=Q\,h(D)\,Q^T$, so the eigenvalues of $A^m$ are the real numbers $h(\mu_j)$. On the other hand the eigenvalues of $A^m$ are $\lambda_i^m$. Hence for each $i$ there is a real $\mu$ with
$$\lambda_i^m=2021\mu-\mu^2=\frac{2021^2}{4}-\Big(\mu-\frac{2021}{2}\Big)^2\le\frac{2021^2}4 .$$
Take $m$ even: $|\lambda_i|^m\le\frac{2021^2}4$ for all even $m$. If $|\lambda_i|>1$, then $|\lambda_i|^m\to\infty$ along even $m$, a contradiction. So $|\lambda_i|\le1$ for all $i$, and
$$|\det A|=|\lambda_1|\cdots|\lambda_n|\le1 .$$
∎

solutions.title: Complete the square
solutions.body:
As in the first solution, $m=1$ gives that $A=2021B_1-B_1^2$ is real symmetric, so it has an orthonormal basis of real eigenvectors.

For any $m$, completing the square,
$$\frac{2021^2}{4}I-A^m=\Big(B_m-\frac{2021}{2}I\Big)^2=C^2,\qquad C=B_m-\frac{2021}{2}I=C^T .$$
Let $v$ be a unit eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$. Then
$$\frac{2021^2}{4}-\lambda^m=v^T\Big(\frac{2021^2}{4}I-A^m\Big)v=v^TC^TCv=\|Cv\|^2\ge0 .$$
So $\lambda^{m}\le\frac{2021^2}4$ for every $m$; using even $m=2j$ gives $|\lambda|\le\left(\frac{2021^2}{4}\right)^{1/(2j)}\to1$ as $j\to\infty$, i.e. $|\lambda|\le 1$. Since $|\det A|$ is the product of the $|\lambda|$ over the eigenvalues, $|\det A|\le1$. ∎

prompt: For a prime number $p$, let $GL_2(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)$ be the group of invertible $2\times2$ matrices of residues modulo $p$, and let $S_p$ be the symmetric group (the group of all permutations) on $p$ elements. Show that there is no injective group homomorphism $\phi:GL_2(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)\to S_p$.
answer: For odd $p$, $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\cdot(-I)$ has order $2p$, but $S_p$ has no element of order $2p$ (an element of order divisible by $p$ is a $p$-cycle, of order $p$). For $p=2$ compare orders: $6>2$.

solutions.title: An element of order $2p$
solutions.body:
An injective homomorphism maps every element to an element of the same order (if $\phi(g)^k=1$ then $\phi(g^k)=1$, so $g^k=1$, and conversely). We show $GL_2(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)$ has an element whose order does not occur in $S_p$.

**$p=2$.** $|GL_2(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)|=(4-1)(4-2)=6>2=|S_2|$, so no injective map exists at all.

**$p$ odd.** Let
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Since $A^j=\begin{pmatrix}1&j\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $A$ has order $p$; $B=-I\ne I$ (as $p\ne2$) has order $2$, and $B$ commutes with $A$. Hence $(AB)^j=A^jB^j$, and $(AB)^j=I$ means $A^j=B^{-j}\in\langle A\rangle\cap\langle B\rangle=\{I\}$ (a subgroup of order dividing both $p$ and $2$), i.e. $p\mid j$ and $2\mid j$. So $AB$ has order $2p$.

**No element of $S_p$ has order $2p$.** The order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths, all of which are at most $p$. If $p$ divides the order, then (as $p$ is prime) some cycle length is divisible by $p$, so it equals $p$: the permutation is a single $p$-cycle using all $p$ points, and its order is exactly $p\ne2p$.

Therefore $\phi(AB)$ would be an element of order $2p$ in $S_p$, which does not exist. So no injective homomorphism exists. ∎

solutions.title: Centralisers
solutions.body:
($p=2$ is handled by counting: $|GL_2(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)|=6>2$.) Let $p$ be odd and suppose $\phi$ is injective.

Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, of order $p$. Then $\sigma=\phi(A)\in S_p$ has order $p$, so, as in the first solution, $\sigma$ is a $p$-cycle, say $\sigma=(1\,2\,\dots\,p)$ after renaming points.

**The centraliser of a $p$-cycle is $\langle\sigma\rangle$.** If $\tau\sigma=\sigma\tau$, then $\tau(\sigma^i(1))=\sigma^i(\tau(1))$ for all $i$; writing $\tau(1)=\sigma^r(1)$ gives $\tau=\sigma^r$. So the centraliser has exactly $p$ elements.

**The centraliser of $A$ is bigger.** The scalar matrices $cI$ ($c\ne0$) and the powers of $A$ commute with $A$; the products $cA^j$ ($c\in(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^*$, $0\le j<p$) are $p(p-1)$ distinct matrices, all commuting with $A$. Since $p-1\ge2$, this is more than $p$.

Because $\phi$ is injective, it maps the centraliser of $A$ injectively into the centraliser of $\sigma$ (if $XA=AX$ then $\phi(X)\sigma=\sigma\phi(X)$). This would give $p(p-1)\le p$, a contradiction. ∎

prompt:
Let $D\subseteq\mathbb C$ be an open set containing the closed unit disk $\{z:|z|\le1\}$. Let $f:D\to\mathbb C$ be a holomorphic function, and let $p(z)$ be a monic polynomial. Prove that
$$|f(0)|\le\max_{|z|=1}|f(z)p(z)| .$$
answer: Let $q(z)=z^n\,\overline{p(1/\bar z)}=1+\overline{a_{n-1}}z+\dots+\overline{a_0}z^n$. Then $q(0)=1$ and $|q|=|p|$ on $|z|=1$, so the maximum principle for $fq$ gives $|f(0)|=|f(0)q(0)|\le\max_{|z|=1}|fq|=\max_{|z|=1}|fp|$.

solutions.title: Reverse the polynomial
solutions.body:
Write $p(z)=z^n+a_{n-1}z^{n-1}+\dots+a_1z+a_0$ with complex $a_j$, and define the "reversed conjugate" polynomial
$$q(z)=1+\overline{a_{n-1}}\,z+\overline{a_{n-2}}\,z^2+\dots+\overline{a_0}\,z^n .$$
Then $q(0)=1$. For $|z|=1$ we have $\bar z=1/z$, hence
$$z^n\,\overline{p(z)}=z^n\big(\bar z^{\,n}+\overline{a_{n-1}}\,\bar z^{\,n-1}+\dots+\overline{a_0}\big)=1+\overline{a_{n-1}}z+\dots+\overline{a_0}z^n=q(z),$$
so $|q(z)|=|z|^n|p(z)|=|p(z)|$ on the unit circle.

The function $F=f\cdot q$ is holomorphic on $D$, which contains the closed unit disk. By the maximum modulus principle (or by Cauchy's formula $F(0)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}F(e^{i\theta})\,d\theta$),
$$|f(0)|=|F(0)|\le\max_{|z|=1}|F(z)|=\max_{|z|=1}|f(z)|\,|q(z)|=\max_{|z|=1}|f(z)p(z)| .$$
∎

solutions.title: Factor into roots
solutions.body:
Factor $p(z)=\prod_{j=1}^n(z-z_j)$. For $|z|=1$,
$$|z-z_j|=|\bar z|\,|z-z_j|=|\bar zz-z_j\bar z|=|1-z_j\bar z|=\big|\overline{1-z_j\bar z}\big|=|1-\overline{z_j}\,z| .$$ Hence $Q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^n(1-\overline{z_j}z)$ is a polynomial with $Q(0)=1$ and $|Q(z)|=|p(z)|$ for $|z|=1$.

Apply the Cauchy integral formula to the holomorphic function $fQ$ on the unit circle:
$$f(0)=f(0)Q(0)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(e^{i\theta})Q(e^{i\theta})\,d\theta ,$$
so
$$|f(0)|\le\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(e^{i\theta})|\,|p(e^{i\theta})|\,d\theta\le\max_{|z|=1}|f(z)p(z)| .$$
∎

prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer. At most how many distinct unit vectors can be selected in $\mathbb R^n$ such that from any three of them, at least two are orthogonal?
answer: 2n

solutions.title: Traces of sums of projections
solutions.body:
**Answer: $2n$.**

**Example.** Take $\pm e_1,\dots,\pm e_n$ (a basis and its negatives): $2n$ distinct unit vectors. Among any three of them two have different indices (each index occurs only twice), and those two are orthogonal.

**Upper bound.** Let $v_1,\dots,v_N$ be unit vectors with the property, and let $P_i=v_iv_i^T$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb Rv_i$. Then $P_i^2=P_i$, $\operatorname{tr}P_i=1$, and for $i\ne j$, $\operatorname{tr}(P_iP_j)=(v_i\cdot v_j)^2=:c_{ij}$. For distinct $i,j,k$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(P_iP_jP_k)=(v_i\cdot v_j)(v_j\cdot v_k)(v_k\cdot v_i)=0,$$
since one of the three dot products vanishes.

Let $Q=\sum_iP_i$. It is symmetric positive semidefinite with eigenvalues $t_1,\dots,t_n\ge0$, and $\sum t_r=\operatorname{tr}Q=N$. Expanding,
$$\operatorname{tr}Q^2=\sum_i\operatorname{tr}P_i^2+\sum_{i\ne j}\operatorname{tr}P_iP_j=N+2\sum_{i<j}c_{ij}.$$
In $\operatorname{tr}Q^3=\sum_{i,j,k}\operatorname{tr}(P_iP_jP_k)$, triples with three distinct indices contribute $0$; triples $(i,i,i)$ contribute $\operatorname{tr}P_i=1$ each; and for each pair $i<j$ the six triples using exactly the indices $i,j$ each contribute $\operatorname{tr}(P_iP_j)=c_{ij}$ (by $P^2=P$ and cyclicity of the trace). Hence
$$\operatorname{tr}Q^3=N+6\sum_{i<j}c_{ij}=N+3(\operatorname{tr}Q^2-N)=3\operatorname{tr}Q^2-2N .$$
In terms of eigenvalues: $\sum_r(t_r^3-3t_r^2)=-2N$. But for $t\ge0$,
$$t^3-3t^2+4=(t-2)^2(t+1)\ge0,$$
so $\sum_r(t_r^3-3t_r^2)\ge-4n$. Therefore $-2N\ge-4n$, i.e. $N\le2n$.

**Answer: $2n$.** ∎

solutions.title: Gram matrix and Hölder
solutions.body:
The example $\pm e_1,\dots,\pm e_n$ shows $2n$ is possible. Suppose there were $N=2n+1$ such vectors $v_1,\dots,v_N$.

Let $G=(v_i\cdot v_j)$ be their Gram matrix and $B=G-I$ (same off-diagonal entries, zero diagonal). $G$ is positive semidefinite of rank at most $n$, so $B$ has real eigenvalues $\ge-1$, and $-1$ is an eigenvalue of multiplicity at least $N-n=n+1$. The positive eigenvalues $x_1,\dots,x_m$ of $B$ correspond to eigenvalues $>1$ of $G$, so $m\le n$. Let $y_1,\dots,y_s\in[-1,0)$ be the negative eigenvalues; at least $n+1$ of them equal $-1$.

* $\operatorname{tr}B=0$: $\sum x_i=\sum|y_j|$.
* $\operatorname{tr}B^3=\sum_{i,j,k}b_{ij}b_{jk}b_{ki}$; only terms with $i\ne j\ne k\ne i$ survive (zero diagonal), and each is $(v_i\cdot v_j)(v_j\cdot v_k)(v_k\cdot v_i)=0$. So $\sum x_i^3=\sum|y_j|^3$.

Since $|y_j|\le1$, $\sum|y_j|^3\le\sum|y_j|$, hence $\sum x_i^3\le\sum x_i$. Also $\sum x_i^3=\sum|y_j|^3\ge n+1$. By Hölder (power-mean) inequality, $\sum x_i^3\ge\frac{(\sum x_i)^3}{m^2}$. Combining,
$$\sum x_i\ \ge\ \sum x_i^3\ \ge\ \frac{(\sum x_i)^3}{m^2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sum x_i\le m\le n,$$
while $\sum x_i\ge\sum x_i^3\ge n+1$. Contradiction. So at most $2n$ vectors can be chosen.

**Answer: $2n$.** ∎

prompt:
Let $f:[0,1]\to(0,\infty)$ be an integrable function such that $f(x)\cdot f(1-x)=1$ for all $x\in[0,1]$. Prove that
$$\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\ge1 .$$
answer: By AM-GM, $f(x)+f(1-x)\ge2\sqrt{f(x)f(1-x)}=2$; integrate over $[0,\frac12]$.

solutions.title: AM-GM on symmetric pairs
solutions.body:
For every $x\in[0,1]$, by the AM-GM inequality and the hypothesis,
$$f(x)+f(1-x)\ge2\sqrt{f(x)f(1-x)}=2 .$$
Split the integral at $\frac12$ and substitute $x\mapsto1-x$ in the second half:
$$\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=\int_0^{1/2}f(x)\,dx+\int_{1/2}^1f(x)\,dx=\int_0^{1/2}\big(f(x)+f(1-x)\big)\,dx\ge\int_0^{1/2}2\,dx=1 .$$
∎

solutions.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
solutions.body:
Let $I=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx>0$. Substituting $x\mapsto1-x$ and using $f(1-x)=1/f(x)$,
$$I=\int_0^1f(1-x)\,dx=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{f(x)} .$$
(In particular $1/f$ is integrable.) By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$I^2=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\cdot\int_0^1\frac{dx}{f(x)}\ge\left(\int_0^1\sqrt{f(x)}\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{f(x)}}\,dx\right)^2=1 .$$
Since $I>0$, $I\ge1$. ∎

answer: Only $A=0$. Transposing gives $A^k\big(I+(I+A^{k-1})^k\big)=0$, whose polynomial has $0$ as its only real root; so $A$ is nilpotent, $A^k=0$, $A=A^T$ is symmetric nilpotent, hence $0$.

solutions.title: An annihilating polynomial
solutions.body:
**Answer: only the zero matrix.** Clearly $A=0$ works.

Conversely, let $A$ satisfy $A^T=A+A^k$ with $k\ge n$. Transposing, $A=A^T+(A^T)^k$, and substituting $A^T=A+A^k$:
$$A=A+A^k+(A+A^k)^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A^k+\big(A(I+A^{k-1})\big)^k=0 .$$
The factors $A$ and $I+A^{k-1}$ commute, so this reads
$$A^k\Big(I+\big(I+A^{k-1}\big)^k\Big)=0 .$$
Thus $p(x)=x^k\big(1+(1+x^{k-1})^k\big)$ annihilates $A$. If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue with eigenvector $v\ne0$, then $0=p(A)v=p(\lambda)v$, so $p(\lambda)=0$.

All eigenvalues of $A$ are real, and for real $x$ the second factor of $p$ is positive: if $k$ is even, $(1+x^{k-1})^k\ge0$; if $k$ is odd, $k-1$ is even, so $1+x^{k-1}\ge1$. Hence every eigenvalue is $0$.

So the characteristic polynomial of $A$ is $x^n$, and by Cayley–Hamilton $A^n=0$; as $k\ge n$, $A^k=0$ and therefore $A^T=A$. A real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalisable, $A=QDQ^T$, and $D$ has the eigenvalues (all $0$) on its diagonal, so $A=0$. ∎

solutions.title: Eigenvalues map to eigenvalues
solutions.body:
$A=0$ works; let $A$ be any solution with $k\ge n$.

If $\lambda$ is a (real) eigenvalue of $A$ with real eigenvector $v$, then $A^Tv=Av+A^kv=(\lambda+\lambda^k)v$, so $\lambda+\lambda^k$ is an eigenvalue of $A^T$, hence of $A$ (same characteristic polynomial).

* **$k$ odd.** Take an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of largest absolute value. If $\lambda\ne0$, then $|\lambda+\lambda^k|=|\lambda|\,(1+\lambda^{k-1})>|\lambda|$ (as $k-1$ is even), contradicting maximality. So all eigenvalues are $0$.
* **$k$ even.** Taking traces in $A^T=A+A^k$ gives $\operatorname{tr}A^k=0$, i.e. $\sum\lambda_i^k=0$ over the (real) eigenvalues with multiplicity. Each term is $\ge0$ as $k$ is even, so all $\lambda_i=0$.

Hence $A$ is nilpotent, $A^n=0$ (Cayley–Hamilton), so $A^k=0$ and $A=A^T$. A symmetric matrix with all eigenvalues $0$ is $0$ (it is orthogonally diagonalisable). **Answer: $A=0$.** ∎

prompt: Let $p$ be a prime number. A flea is staying at point $0$ of the real line. At each minute, the flea has three possibilities: to stay at its position, or to move by $1$ to the left or to the right. After $p-1$ minutes, it wants to be at $0$ again. Denote by $f(p)$ the number of its strategies to do this (for example, $f(3)=3$: it may either stay at $0$ for the entire time, or go to the left and then to the right, or go to the right and then to the left). Find $f(p)$ modulo $p$.
answer: $f(p)\equiv0$ if $p=3$, $f(p)\equiv1$ if $p\equiv1\pmod 3$, and $f(p)\equiv-1$ if $p\equiv2\pmod3$ (all modulo $p$).

solutions.title: Generating function over $\mathbb F_p$
solutions.body:
**Answer:** modulo $p$, $f(p)\equiv0$ for $p=3$, $f(p)\equiv1$ for $p\equiv1\pmod3$, and $f(p)\equiv-1$ for $p\equiv2\pmod3$.

A strategy is a sequence of $p-1$ moves from $\{-1,0,+1\}$ with sum $0$. Encoding the moves by $x^{-1},1,x$, $f(p)$ is the constant term of $(x^{-1}+1+x)^{p-1}$, i.e.
$$f(p)=[x^{p-1}]\,(1+x+x^2)^{p-1}.$$
Work with formal power series with coefficients in $\mathbb F_p$. Since $1+x+x^2=\frac{1-x^3}{1-x}$,
$$(1+x+x^2)^{p-1}=\frac{(1-x^3)^{p}}{1-x^3}\cdot\frac{1-x}{(1-x)^{p}}=\frac{(1-x^{3p})(1-x)}{(1-x^3)(1-x^p)},$$
using $(1-y)^p=1-y^p$ in characteristic $p$. Modulo $x^p$ we have $1-x^{3p}\equiv1$ and $\frac1{1-x^p}\equiv1$, and we only need the coefficient of $x^{p-1}$. Hence
$$f(p)\equiv[x^{p-1}]\,\frac{1-x}{1-x^3}=[x^{p-1}]\,(1-x)\sum_{j\ge0}x^{3j}=c(p-1)-c(p-2)\pmod p,$$
where $c(i)=1$ if $3\mid i$ and $0$ otherwise.

* $p\equiv1\pmod3$: $c(p-1)-c(p-2)=1-0=1$.
* $p\equiv2\pmod3$ (including $p=2$): $0-1=-1$.
* $p=3$: $c(2)-c(1)=0$ (indeed $f(3)=3\equiv0$).

∎

solutions.title: Cyclic shifts and a linear system
solutions.body:
($p=2$: the only strategy is to stay, $f(2)=1\equiv-1\pmod2$; $p=3$: $f(3)=3\equiv0$. Let $p\ge5$.)

For a residue $i$ mod $p$ and $t\ge0$ let $a_i(t)$ be the number of $t$-move strategies ending at a position $\equiv i\pmod p$. After $p-1$ moves the position lies in $[-(p-1),p-1]$, so it is $\equiv0$ only if it is $0$: $f(p)=a_0(p-1)$. Also $a_i(t+1)=a_{i-1}(t)+a_i(t)+a_{i+1}(t)$ (indices mod $p$), according to the last move.

**Strategies of length $p$.** The cyclic group $\mathbb Z/p$ acts on sequences of $p$ moves by rotation, preserving the sum. A non-constant sequence has an orbit of size exactly $p$ (the stabiliser is a proper subgroup of a group of prime order). The three constant sequences all end at a position $\equiv0$ ($0$, $p$, $-p$). Hence $a_0(p)\equiv3$ and $a_i(p)\equiv0$ for $i\ne0$, modulo $p$.

So $x_i=a_i(p-1)$ satisfies, modulo $p$,
$$x_{i-1}+x_i+x_{i+1}\equiv3\delta_{i,0}\qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p).$$
**Uniqueness.** Let $S$ be the cyclic shift on $\mathbb F_p^{\,p}$. Then $S^p=I$, so $(S-I)^p=S^p-I=0$ (characteristic $p$): $S=I+N$ with $N$ nilpotent. Since $S^{-1}=(I+N)^{-1}=I-N+N^2-\dots$, the system matrix is $S^{-1}+I+S=3I+N'$, where $N'$ is a polynomial in $N$ without constant term and hence nilpotent; so it is invertible because $3\ne0$ in $\mathbb F_p$. So the system has exactly one solution mod $p$.

**The solution.** If $p=3m+1$, take $x_i=1$ for $i\equiv0,1\pmod3$ and $x_i=-2$ for $i\equiv2\pmod 3$ ($0\le i\le p-1$). Any three cyclically consecutive entries inside $0..p-1$ sum to $0$; at the wrap-around, $x_{p-1}+x_0+x_1=1+1+1=3$ and $x_{p-2}+x_{p-1}+x_0=-2+1+1=0$. So this is the solution and $f(p)\equiv x_0=1$.

If $p=3m+2$, take $x_i=-1,2,-1$ for $i\equiv0,1,2\pmod3$. Interior triples sum to $0$; $x_{p-1}+x_0+x_1=2-1+2=3$ and $x_{p-2}+x_{p-1}+x_0=-1+2-1=0$. So $f(p)\equiv x_0=-1$.

**Answer:** $f(p)\equiv1$ if $p\equiv1\pmod3$, $f(p)\equiv-1$ if $p\equiv2\pmod 3$, $f(3)\equiv0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n>3$ be an integer. Let $\Omega$ be the set of all triples of distinct elements of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$. Let $m$ denote the minimal number of colours which suffice to colour $\Omega$ so that whenever $1\le a<b<c<d\le n$, the triples $\{a,b,c\}$ and $\{b,c,d\}$ have different colours. Prove that
$$\frac1{100}\log\log n\le m\le100\log\log n .$$
answer: Shift graphs: with $G_k$ the digraph on $k$-subsets ($\{a_1<\dots<a_k\}\to\{a_2<\dots<a_{k+1}\}$), $\chi(G_k)=b(G_{k-1})$ where $b$ is the least number of "no directed 2-path" edge classes, and $\log_2\chi(G)\le b(G)\le2\lceil\log_2\chi(G)\rceil$. Since $\chi(G_1)=n$, $\log_2\log_2n\le m=\chi(G_3)\le2\lceil\log_2\lceil\log_2n\rceil\rceil$.

solutions.title: Shift graphs and binary colourings
solutions.body:
Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm. We prove the sharper bounds
$$\log_2\log_2n\ \le\ m\ \le\ 2\big\lceil\log_2\lceil\log_2n\rceil\big\rceil .\tag{$*$}$$

**Shift graphs.** For $k\ge1$ let $G_k$ be the directed graph whose vertices are the $k$-subsets of $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, with an edge $\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}\to\{a_2,\dots,a_{k+1}\}$ for each $(k+1)$-subset $a_1<\dots<a_{k+1}$. Edges of $G_k$ are thus in bijection with $(k+1)$-subsets. The required colourings of $\Omega$ are exactly the proper vertex colourings of $G_3$, so $m=\chi(G_3)$.

Call a set $E_1$ of edges of a digraph **admissible** if it contains no directed path $u\to v\to w$ of two edges, and let $b(G)$ be the minimum number of admissible sets covering all edges.

**Lemma 1.** A set of $k$-subsets is independent in $G_k$ iff, as a set of edges of $G_{k-1}$, it is admissible. Hence $\chi(G_k)=b(G_{k-1})$ for $k\ge2$.

*Proof.* A directed 2-path in $G_{k-1}$ is $\{a_1..a_{k-1}\}\to\{a_2..a_k\}\to\{a_3..a_{k+1}\}$ for some $a_1<\dots<a_{k+1}$; its two edges are the $k$-sets $\{a_1..a_k\}$ and $\{a_2..a_{k+1}\}$, which are exactly the endpoints of an edge of $G_k$, and every edge of $G_k$ arises this way. So "no 2-path inside the set" is the same as "no edge inside the set". Covering by independent sets is the same as colouring (subsets of independent/admissible sets stay so), so $\chi(G_k)=b(G_{k-1})$. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** For every digraph $G$ without loops, $\log_2\chi(G)\le b(G)\le2\lceil\log_2\chi(G)\rceil$.

*Proof.* (Lower bound.) Let $E_1,\dots,E_b$ be admissible sets covering the edges. Colour each vertex $v$ by the set $c(v)=\{i:\ v\text{ has an outgoing edge in }E_i\}\subseteq[b]$. For an edge $v\to w$, pick $i$ with $v\to w\in E_i$; then $i\in c(v)$, and $i\notin c(w)$, since an edge $w\to u$ in $E_i$ would form a 2-path $v\to w\to u$ in $E_i$. So $c(v)\ne c(w)$, $c$ is a proper colouring with at most $2^b$ colours, and $\chi(G)\le2^{b}$.

(Upper bound.) Let $\chi(G)=q$, $\tau:V\to\{0,\dots,q-1\}$ a proper colouring and $r=\lceil\log_2q\rceil$, so every colour has an $r$-bit binary expansion; let $\varepsilon_i(x)$ be bit $i$ of $x$. For $i=0,\dots,r-1$ set
$$E_{i,+}=\{v\to u:\ \varepsilon_i(\tau(v))=0,\ \varepsilon_i(\tau(u))=1\},\qquad E_{i,-}=\{v\to u:\ \varepsilon_i(\tau(v))=1,\ \varepsilon_i(\tau(u))=0\}.$$
A 2-path $v\to w\to u$ inside $E_{i,+}$ would need bit $i$ of $\tau(w)$ to be both $1$ and $0$; so each set is admissible (same for $E_{i,-}$). Every edge $v\to u$ has $\tau(v)\ne\tau(u)$, so they differ in some bit $i$ and the edge lies in $E_{i,+}$ or $E_{i,-}$. Thus $b(G)\le2r$. $\square$

**Putting it together.** $G_1$ has vertices $1,\dots,n$ and an edge $i\to j$ for all $i<j$, so $\chi(G_1)=n$. Moreover $b(G_1)\le\lceil\log_2n\rceil$: with $\tau(v)=v-1$, for $v<u$ the highest bit where $v-1$ and $u-1$ differ is $0$ in $v-1$ and $1$ in $u-1$, so the $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ sets $E_{i,+}$ already cover all edges. Using Lemmas 1 and 2:
$$\chi(G_2)=b(G_1)\in\big[\log_2n,\ \lceil\log_2n\rceil\big],$$
$$m=\chi(G_3)=b(G_2)\ \ge\ \log_2\chi(G_2)\ \ge\ \log_2\log_2n,\qquad m=b(G_2)\le2\lceil\log_2\chi(G_2)\rceil\le2\big\lceil\log_2\lceil\log_2n\rceil\big\rceil .$$
This is $(*)$.

**The stated bounds.** Let $L=\log\log n$; for $n\ge4$, $L\ge\log\log4>0.32$. Since $\log_2\log_2n=\frac{L-\log\log2}{\log2}=\frac{L+0.366\ldots}{0.693\ldots}\ge L$, the lower bound gives $m\ge L\ge\frac{L}{100}$. For the upper bound, $\lceil\log_2n\rceil\le2\log_2n$ and $\lceil y\rceil\le y+1$, so
$$m\le2\big(\log_2(2\log_2n)+1\big)=4+2\log_2\log_2n\le4+2\cdot\frac{L+0.37}{0.69}<5.1+2.9L .$$
As $L>0.32$, $5.1<16L$, so $m<19L\le100L$. Hence $\frac1{100}\log\log n\le m\le100\log\log n$. ∎

prompt: We colour all the sides and diagonals of a regular polygon $P$ with $43$ vertices either red or blue in such a way that every vertex is an endpoint of $20$ red segments and $22$ blue segments. A triangle formed by vertices of $P$ is called *monochromatic* if all of its sides have the same colour. Suppose that there are $2022$ blue monochromatic triangles. How many red monochromatic triangles are there?

solutions.title: Double-count cherries
solutions.body:
Call a pair of segments sharing a vertex a *cherry*; it is monochromatic if both segments have the same colour. Every cherry lies in exactly one triangle. A monochromatic triangle contains $3$ monochromatic cherries; any other triangle has two sides of one colour and one of the other, so it contains exactly $1$ monochromatic and $2$ bichromatic cherries.

Let $M$ and $B$ be the numbers of monochromatic and bichromatic cherries. Then each monochromatic triangle contributes $2\cdot3-0=6$ to $2M-B$ and each other triangle contributes $2\cdot1-2=0$, so
$$2M-B=6T,$$
where $T$ is the number of monochromatic triangles.

At each vertex there are $\binom{20}2+\binom{22}2=190+231=421$ monochromatic and $20\cdot22=440$ bichromatic cherries, so $2M-B=43\,(2\cdot421-440)=43\cdot402$. Hence
$$T=\frac{43\cdot402}{6}=43\cdot67=2881,$$
and the number of red monochromatic triangles is $2881-2022=859$.

**Answer: $859$.**

solutions.title: Count non-monochromatic triangles
solutions.body:
There are $\binom{43}3=12341$ triangles. A non-monochromatic triangle has exactly two vertices at which its two sides have different colours (the vertex opposite the odd-coloured side has two equal sides). At each vertex the number of pairs (red segment, blue segment) is $20\cdot22=440$, and each such pair spans exactly one triangle. So
$$\#\{\text{non-monochromatic}\}=\frac{43\cdot440}{2}=9460,$$
the number of monochromatic triangles is $12341-9460=2881$, and the red ones number $2881-2022=859$.

**Answer: $859$.**

prompt:
Let $p>2$ be a prime number. Prove that there is a permutation $(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{p-1})$ of the numbers $(1,2,\dots,p-1)$ such that
$$x_1x_2+x_2x_3+\dots+x_{p-2}x_{p-1}\equiv2\pmod p .$$
answer: Take $x_i\equiv i^{-1}\pmod p$; then the sum telescopes: $\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}\frac1{i(i+1)}=1-\frac1{p-1}\equiv1+1=2$.

solutions.title: Use inverses: a telescoping sum
solutions.body:
Let $x_i\in\{1,\dots,p-1\}$ be the inverse of $i$ modulo $p$, for $i=1,\dots,p-1$. Inversion is a bijection of the nonzero residues, so $(x_1,\dots,x_{p-1})$ is a permutation of $(1,\dots,p-1)$. Computing modulo $p$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}x_ix_{i+1}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}\frac1{i(i+1)}=\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}\Big(\frac1i-\frac1{i+1}\Big)=1-\frac1{p-1}\equiv1-\frac1{-1}=2\pmod p .$$
(The partial-fraction identity holds in the field $\mathbb F_p$ because $i,i+1\not\equiv0$ for $1\le i\le p-2$.) ∎

solutions.title: Perturb the identity permutation
solutions.body:
For $p=3$ take $(1,2)$: the sum is $2$. Let $p\ge5$.

The identity permutation gives
$$\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}i(i+1)=\frac{(p-2)(p-1)p}{3}\equiv0\pmod p$$
(as $3\nmid p$, the factor $p$ survives). Replacing a block $(i,i+1,i+2,i+3)$ of consecutive values by $(i,i+2,i+1,i+3)$ changes the three products in it from $i(i+1)+(i+1)(i+2)+(i+2)(i+3)$ to $i(i+2)+(i+2)(i+1)+(i+1)(i+3)$, a **decrease by $3$**. Blocks on disjoint sets of adjacent pairs act independently.

* **$p\equiv2\pmod3$:** swap $3j-1$ and $3j$ for $j=1,\dots,\frac{p-2}3$ (blocks starting at $1,4,7,\dots,p-4$; they use disjoint adjacent pairs). The sum decreases by $3\cdot\frac{p-2}3=p-2$, giving $-(p-2)\equiv2$.
* **$p\equiv1\pmod3$, $p\ge13$:** first replace $(1,2,3,4,5)$ by $(1,4,3,2,5)$: the products $2+6+12+20=40$ become $4+12+6+10=32$, a decrease of $8$. Then swap $3j$ and $3j+1$ for $j=2,\dots,\frac{p-7}3$ (blocks starting at $5,8,\dots,p-8$), each decreasing by $3$, in total $p-10$. The sum becomes $-8-(p-10)\equiv2$.
* **$p=7$:** $(1,4,5,2,3,6)$ gives $4+20+10+6+18=58\equiv2\pmod7$.

In all cases a suitable permutation exists. ∎

prompt:
Let $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_k$ be $n\times n$ idempotent complex matrices such that
$$A_iA_j=-A_jA_i\quad\text{for all }i\ne j.$$
Prove that at least one of the given matrices has rank $\le\frac nk$. (A matrix $A$ is called idempotent if $A^2=A$.)
answer: $\sum A_i$ is again idempotent, and for idempotents rank $=$ trace, so $\sum\operatorname{rank}A_i=\operatorname{tr}\sum A_i=\operatorname{rank}\sum A_i\le n$.

solutions.title: Rank equals trace
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** For an idempotent matrix $B$, $\operatorname{rank}B=\operatorname{tr}B$.

*Proof.* $B$ is annihilated by $x^2-x=x(x-1)$, which has distinct roots, so $B$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues in $\{0,1\}$. The rank is the number of nonzero eigenvalues (with multiplicity), i.e. the number of eigenvalues equal to $1$, which is the trace. $\square$

**The sum is idempotent.** Let $S=A_1+\dots+A_k$. Then
$$S^2=\sum_iA_i^2+\sum_{i<j}(A_iA_j+A_jA_i)=\sum_iA_i=S .$$
By the lemma (applied to each $A_i$ and to $S$) and linearity of the trace,
$$\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{rank}A_i=\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{tr}A_i=\operatorname{tr}S=\operatorname{rank}S\le n .$$
Hence the smallest of the $k$ ranks is at most $\frac nk$. ∎

solutions.title: The images form a direct sum
solutions.body:
**Step 1: $A_iA_j=0$ for $i\ne j$.** Let $A=A_i$, $B=A_j$. Using $A^2=A$ and $AB=-BA$ repeatedly:
$$AB=A(AB)=A(-BA)=-(AB)A=(BA)A=BA .$$
Together with $AB=-BA$ this gives $2AB=0$, so $AB=BA=0$.

**Step 2: the images are independent.** Let $V_i=\operatorname{im}A_i$; note $A_iv=v$ for $v\in V_i$ (if $v=A_iw$ then $A_iv=A_i^2w=v$). Suppose $v_1+\dots+v_k=0$ with $v_i\in V_i$. Apply $A_j$: for $i\ne j$, $A_jv_i=A_jA_iw_i=0$, while $A_jv_j=v_j$. So $v_j=0$ for every $j$. Hence the sum $V_1+\dots+V_k$ is direct and
$$\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{rank}A_i=\sum_{i=1}^k\dim V_i=\dim(V_1\oplus\dots\oplus V_k)\le n .$$
So some $\operatorname{rank}A_i\le\frac nk$. ∎

prompt: Let $n,k\ge3$ be integers, and let $S$ be a circle. Let $n$ blue points and $k$ red points be chosen uniformly and independently at random on the circle $S$. Denote by $F$ the intersection of the convex hull of the red points and the convex hull of the blue points. Let $m$ be the number of vertices of the convex polygon $F$ (in particular, $m=0$ when $F$ is empty). Find the expected value of $m$.
answer:
$$\mathbb E(m)=\frac{2kn}{n+k-1}-\frac{2\,k!\,n!}{(n+k-1)!}$$
($m$ equals the number of colour changes around the circle, except that it is $0$ instead of $2$ when each colour forms one arc).

solutions.title: Count colour changes around the circle
solutions.body:
**Answer:** $\displaystyle\mathbb E(m)=\frac{2kn}{n+k-1}-\frac{2\,k!\,n!}{(n+k-1)!}$.

With probability $1$ all $n+k$ points are distinct and no three chords through them are concurrent; we assume this. Let $R$ and $B$ be the red and blue convex polygons. Going around the circle, the colours form $2s$ maximal monochromatic runs, alternating red and blue ($s\ge1$); the number of colour changes is $2s$.

**Geometric step: $m=0$ if $s=1$, and $m=2s$ if $s\ge2$.** The edges of $R$ join cyclically consecutive red points $r,r'$. Call such an edge *long* if the arc from $r$ to $r'$ containing no other red point contains blue points (then it contains a whole blue run), and *short* otherwise. There is one long red edge per blue run, i.e. $s$ of them; similarly $s$ long blue edges.

* If $s=1$, the red points fill one arc and the blue points the complementary arc; the line through the long red edge has all red points on one closed side and all blue points strictly on the other side. So $B$ lies in an open half-plane disjoint from the closed half-plane containing $R$, hence $F=\varnothing$ and $m=0$.
* Let $s\ge2$. For a short red edge all blue points lie strictly on one side of its line, the side away from the edge's arc, so this edge does not meet $B$. For a long red edge, its arc contains a blue run and the opposite arc contains another blue run, so its line separates blue points and the chord passes through the interior of $B$; its intersection with $B$ is a non-degenerate segment. The boundary of $F=R\cap B$ consists of the parts of $\partial R$ inside $B$ and of $\partial B$ inside $R$. Each edge line meets the convex set $F$ in at most one segment, so each long edge contributes exactly one side of $F$, short edges none, and different edges lie on different lines. Hence $F$ has $2s$ sides and $m=2s$.

So $m$ equals the number $C$ of colour changes, minus $2$ in the exceptional event $\mathcal E$ that $s=1$.

**Probabilistic step.** Cut the circle at a fixed point and read the colours $C_1,\dots,C_{n+k}$ counterclockwise (cyclically, $C_{n+k}$ is adjacent to $C_1$). All $\binom{n+k}{n}$ colour patterns are equally likely (choose the $n+k$ positions first, then the colours are a uniformly random arrangement). For each of the $n+k$ cyclically adjacent pairs,
$$P(\text{colour change})=\frac{2nk}{(n+k)(n+k-1)},$$
so by linearity $\mathbb E\,C=\frac{2nk}{n+k-1}$. The event $\mathcal E$ consists of the $n+k$ patterns in which the red positions form a cyclic interval (choose where it starts), so
$$P(\mathcal E)=\frac{n+k}{\binom{n+k}{n}}=\frac{n!\,k!}{(n+k-1)!}.$$
Therefore
$$\mathbb E(m)=\mathbb E\,C-2P(\mathcal E)=\frac{2nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{2\,n!\,k!}{(n+k-1)!}.$$
∎
(For example, $n=k=3$ gives $\frac{18}5-\frac{72}{120}=3$.)

solutions.title: Each blue point's outgoing edge
solutions.body:
(Using the geometric description from the first solution: an edge of either polygon contributes one side of $F$ unless all points of the other colour lie on one side of it.)

Label the blue points $A_1,\dots,A_n$. For each $A_i$ let $A_iA'_i$ be the blue edge leaving $A_i$ counterclockwise, and let $b_i=1$ if this edge contains a side of $F$, else $0$; define $r_1,\dots,r_k$ similarly for red points. Then $m=\sum b_i+\sum r_j$.

Read the other $n+k-1$ points counterclockwise from $A_i$; their colour pattern is uniform among the $\binom{n+k-1}{k}$ choices of red positions. The edge $A_iA'_i$ fails to contain a side of $F$ iff all red points are on one side of it, which happens iff either
* the next point after $A_i$ is blue (edge is short): probability $\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}$; or
* the next $k$ points are all red and then come the $n-1$ remaining blue points: probability $1/\binom{n+k-1}{k}$.

(These are exclusive; if the edge spans some but not all red points, red points lie on both sides.) Hence
$$\mathbb E\,b_i=1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!\,(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}=\frac{k}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!\,(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!},$$
and symmetrically $\mathbb E\,r_j=\frac{n}{n+k-1}-\frac{n!\,(k-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}$. Summing,
$$\mathbb E(m)=n\,\mathbb E b_1+k\,\mathbb E r_1=\frac{2nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{2\,n!\,k!}{(n+k-1)!}.$$
∎

prompt: Find all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that have a continuous second derivative and for which the equality $f(7x+1)=49f(x)$ holds for all $x\in\mathbb R$.
answer: $f(x)=c(6x+1)^2$ for a real constant $c$ (differentiating twice gives $f''(7x+1)=f''(x)$, so $f''$ is constant by iterating towards the fixed point $-\frac16$).

solutions.title: Differentiate twice and iterate
solutions.body:
**Answer: $f(x)=c(6x+1)^2$, $c\in\mathbb R$.** These work: $c(42x+7)^2=49c(6x+1)^2$.

Conversely, differentiating the identity twice gives $49f''(7x+1)=49f''(x)$, i.e.
$$f''(x)=f''\Big(\frac{x-1}7\Big)\qquad\text{for all }x .$$
Fix $x$ and define $x_0=x$, $x_{j+1}=\frac{x_j-1}{7}$. Then $f''(x_j)=f''(x)$ for all $j$, and
$$x_{j+1}+\frac16=\frac17\Big(x_j+\frac16\Big),$$
so $x_j\to-\frac16$. By continuity of $f''$, $f''(x)=f''(-\frac16)$. Thus $f''$ is constant and $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c_0$.

Substituting: $a(7x+1)^2+b(7x+1)+c_0=49ax^2+(14a+7b)x+(a+b+c_0)$ must equal $49ax^2+49bx+49c_0$. So $14a=42b$ and $a+b=48c_0$, i.e. $a=3b$, $b=12c_0$, $a=36c_0$, and
$$f(x)=c_0(36x^2+12x+1)=c_0(6x+1)^2 .$$
∎

solutions.title: Move the fixed point to the origin
solutions.body:
Put $F(y)=f\big(y-\frac16\big)$. Since $7\big(y-\frac16\big)+1=7y-\frac16$, the equation becomes
$$F(7y)=49F(y)\qquad(y\in\mathbb R),$$
and $F\in C^2$. Setting $y=0$ gives $F(0)=0$; differentiating, $7F'(7y)=49F'(y)$, and $y=0$ gives $F'(0)=0$. By Taylor's theorem, $F(y)/y^2\to\frac{F''(0)}2=:c$ as $y\to0$.

For $y\ne0$ let $G(y)=F(y)/y^2$. Then $G(7y)=\frac{49F(y)}{49y^2}=G(y)$, so $G(y)=G(y/7^j)$ for every $j$, and letting $j\to\infty$, $G(y)=c$. Hence $F(y)=cy^2$ for all $y$ (also at $0$), and
$$f(x)=F\Big(x+\frac16\Big)=c\Big(x+\frac16\Big)^2=\frac{c}{36}(6x+1)^2 .$$
So the solutions are exactly $f(x)=C(6x+1)^2$, $C\in\mathbb R$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be $n\times n$ matrices with complex entries satisfying
$$A^2=B^2=C^2\qquad\text{and}\qquad B^3=ABC+2I .$$
Prove that $A^6=I$.
answer: From $B^3=A^2B=BC^2$: $A(AB-BC)=2I=(BC-AB)C$, so $C=-A$ and $AB+BA$ is invertible; then $ABA=2I-B^3$ commutes with $B$, giving $(AB-BA)(AB+BA)=0$, so $AB=BA$, $B^3=I$ and $A^6=B^6=I$.

solutions.title: Factor $B^3-ABC$ in two ways
solutions.body:
**Step 1: $C=-A$.** Since $B^3=B^2B=A^2B$, the second relation gives $A^2B-ABC=2I$, i.e.
$$A(AB-BC)=2I .$$
Since also $B^3=BB^2=BC^2$, we get $BC^2-ABC=2I$, i.e. $(BC-AB)C=2I$, or
$$(AB-BC)(-C)=2I .$$
So $M=\frac12(AB-BC)$ has left inverse $A$ and right inverse $-C$. Hence $M$ is invertible and $A=M^{-1}=-C$.

**Step 2: $AB=BA$.** With $C=-A$: $M=\frac12(AB+BA)$ is invertible, and $B^3=-ABA+2I$, so $ABA=2I-B^3$ commutes with $B$: $BABA=ABAB$, i.e. $(AB)^2=(BA)^2$. Now
$$(AB-BA)(AB+BA)=(AB)^2+AB^2A-BA^2B-(BA)^2=AB^2A-BA^2B .$$
Using $A^2=B^2$: $AB^2A=A\cdot A^2\cdot A=A^4$ and $BA^2B=B\cdot B^2\cdot B=B^4=(B^2)^2=(A^2)^2=A^4$. So $(AB-BA)(AB+BA)=0$, and since $AB+BA=2M$ is invertible, $AB=BA$.

**Step 3.** Now $ABA=A^2B=B^2B=B^3$, so $B^3=2I-B^3$, i.e. $B^3=I$. Finally
$$A^6=(A^2)^3=(B^2)^3=(B^3)^2=I .$$
∎

prompt:
Find all polynomials $P$ in two variables with real coefficients satisfying the identity
$$P(x,y)P(z,t)=P(xz-yt,\,xt+yz).$$
answer: $P\equiv0$ and $P(x,y)=(x^2+y^2)^n$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$ (in the variables $u=x+iy$, $v=x-iy$ the identity says $P$ is multiplicative, forcing a single monomial $u^av^b$; real coefficients force $a=b$).

solutions.title: Split off the factors $x\pm iy$
solutions.body:
**Answer:** $P\equiv0$ and $P(x,y)=(x^2+y^2)^n$, $n\ge0$. These work, since $(xz-yt)^2+(xt+yz)^2=(x^2+y^2)(z^2+t^2)$.

Note that the identity says $P(w_1)P(w_2)=P(w_1w_2)$ when points $(x,y)$ are read as complex numbers $x+iy$. We first find all solutions with **complex** coefficients. A polynomial identity over $\mathbb R$ in $x,y,z,t$ is also an identity of polynomials.

Let $P\not\equiv0$ and write $P=(x+iy)^n(x-iy)^mQ$ with $n,m\ge0$ and $Q$ divisible by neither $x+iy$ nor $x-iy$ (possible by unique factorisation in $\mathbb C[x,y]$). The polynomial $(x+iy)^n(x-iy)^m$ satisfies the identity itself, because
$$(x+iy)(z+it)=(xz-yt)+i(xt+yz),\qquad (x-iy)(z-it)=(xz-yt)-i(xt+yz).$$
Cancelling these nonzero factors (in the integral domain $\mathbb C[x,y,z,t]$) gives $Q(x,y)Q(z,t)=Q(xz-yt,xt+yz)$.

Put $z=t=0$: $Q(x,y)Q(0,0)=Q(0,0)$. If $Q(0,0)\ne0$, then $Q\equiv1$. Suppose $Q(0,0)=0$. Substitute $x=iy$, $z=-it$: then $xz-yt=yt-yt=0$ and $xt+yz=iyt-iyt=0$, so
$$Q(iy,y)\,Q(-it,t)=Q(0,0)=0\quad\text{for all }y,t .$$
But $Q(iy,y)$ is not the zero polynomial in $y$: writing $Q$ as a polynomial in $w=x-iy$ and $y$, $Q(iy,y)$ is its part free of $w$, which vanishes only if $(x-iy)\mid Q$. Likewise $Q(-it,t)\not\equiv0$ because $(x+iy)\nmid Q$. A product of nonzero polynomials in the independent variables $y$ and $t$ is nonzero — a contradiction.

So the complex solutions are $0$ and $(x+iy)^n(x-iy)^m$. If $P=(x+iy)^n(x-iy)^m$ has real coefficients, then $P=\overline P=(x-iy)^n(x+iy)^m$ as polynomials, and unique factorisation (the two linear factors are non-associate primes) gives $n=m$. Then $P=(x^2+y^2)^n$. ∎

solutions.title: Change variables: $P$ becomes multiplicative
solutions.body:
Work over $\mathbb C$. The substitution $u=x+iy$, $v=x-iy$ is an invertible linear change of variables, so $P(x,y)=\tilde P(u,v)$ for a unique polynomial $\tilde P(u,v)=\sum c_{ab}u^av^b$. The identity holds for all real $x,y,z,t$, hence (being polynomial) for all complex ones. For $(x,y)\leftrightarrow(u_1,v_1)$ and $(z,t)\leftrightarrow(u_2,v_2)$ the point $(xz-yt,xt+yz)$ corresponds to $(u_1u_2,\,v_1v_2)$ (multiply $x\pm iy$ by $z\pm it$). As $(x,y,z,t)$ ranges over $\mathbb C^4$, $(u_1,v_1,u_2,v_2)$ ranges over $\mathbb C^4$, so
$$\tilde P(u_1,v_1)\,\tilde P(u_2,v_2)=\tilde P(u_1u_2,\,v_1v_2)$$
as polynomials. Compare coefficients of $u_1^av_1^bu_2^{a'}v_2^{b'}$: the left side gives $c_{ab}c_{a'b'}$; the right side $\sum c_{ab}u_1^au_2^av_1^bv_2^b$ only has terms with $(a,b)=(a',b')$. So $c_{ab}c_{a'b'}=0$ whenever $(a,b)\ne(a',b')$, and $c_{ab}^2=c_{ab}$. Hence at most one coefficient is nonzero, and it equals $1$: $\tilde P=0$ or $\tilde P=u^av^b$, i.e.
$$P=0\quad\text{or}\quad P=(x+iy)^a(x-iy)^b .$$
If $P$ has real coefficients, then for real $x,y$, $P(x,y)=\overline{P(x,y)}$, so $u^av^b=\bar u^{a}\bar v^{b}=v^au^b$ as polynomials (for real $x,y$, $\bar u=v$), forcing $a=b$. So $P=(uv)^a=(x^2+y^2)^a$.

**Answer:** $P\equiv0$ or $P(x,y)=(x^2+y^2)^n$ with $n\ge0$. ∎

prompt: Let $p$ be a prime number and let $k$ be a positive integer. Suppose that the numbers $a_i=i^k+i$ for $i=0,1,\dots,p-1$ form a complete residue system modulo $p$. What is the set of possible remainders of $a_2$ upon division by $p$?
answer: $a_2\equiv4\pmod p$ always: the set is $\{4\}$ for $p\ge5$ and $\{1\}$ for $p=3$ ($p=2$ is impossible). Key step: $\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}(i^{k-1}+1)\equiv1$ forces $2^{k-1}\equiv1$.

solutions.title: Take the product of all residues
solutions.body:
**Answer:** $a_2\equiv4\pmod p$. So the set of remainders is $\{4\}$ when $p\ge5$ and $\{1\}$ when $p=3$; $p=2$ never occurs.

$p=2$ is impossible since $a_0=0$ and $a_1=2\equiv0$. Let $p$ be odd. The value $k=1$ is admissible ($a_i=2i$ is a complete residue system), and gives $a_2=4$; so it suffices to prove $a_2\equiv4$ in general.

**The product.** Work in $\mathbb F_p$. Since $a_0=0$, the numbers $a_1,\dots,a_{p-1}$ are exactly the nonzero residues, so
$$\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}(i^k+i)=\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}i\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}\big(1+i^{\,m}\big)=1,\qquad m=k-1 .$$

**Evaluating it.** Let $g$ be a primitive root, $h=g^m$, $e$ the order of $h$ and $d=(p-1)/e=\gcd(m,p-1)$ (for $m=0$: $h=1$, $e=1$, $d=p-1$). As $i=g^j$ runs over $j=0,\dots,p-2$, the powers $h^j$ run $d$ times through the $e$ distinct $e$-th roots of unity $1,h,\dots,h^{e-1}$, so
$$\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}(1+i^m)=\Big(\prod_{j=0}^{e-1}(1+h^j)\Big)^{d}.$$
From $\prod_{j=0}^{e-1}(X-h^j)=X^e-1$ at $X=-1$: $(-1)^e\prod_j(1+h^j)=(-1)^e-1$, so $\prod_j(1+h^j)=1-(-1)^e$, which is $0$ if $e$ is even and $2$ if $e$ is odd. The product equals $1\ne0$, so $e$ is odd and $2^d=1$ in $\mathbb F_p$. Since $d\mid m$, also $2^{m}=2^{k-1}\equiv1\pmod p$.

**Conclusion.** $a_2=2^k+2=2\cdot2^{k-1}+2\equiv4\pmod p$. The remainder is $4$ if $p\ge5$ and $4-3=1$ if $p=3$. ∎

prompt:
Fix positive integers $n$ and $k$ such that $2\le k\le n$ and a set $M$ consisting of $n$ fruits. A *permutation* is a sequence $x=(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n)$ such that $\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}=M$. Ivan prefers some (at least one) of these permutations. He realized that for every preferred permutation $x$, there exist $k$ indices $i_1<i_2<\dots<i_k$ with the following property: for every $1\le j<k$, if he swaps $x_{i_j}$ and $x_{i_{j+1}}$, he obtains another preferred permutation.

Prove that he prefers at least $k!$ permutations.
answer: For each permutation $z$ choose a preferred $x$ maximising $\sum_{m\in M}x^{-1}(m)z^{-1}(m)$. The allowed swaps show that then $x_{i_1},\dots,x_{i_k}$ appear in this order in $z$, so each preferred $x$ is chosen by at most $n!/k!$ permutations $z$.

solutions.title: Assign every permutation to a best preferred one
solutions.body:
Let $S$ be the set of all $n!$ permutations and $P\ne\varnothing$ the set of preferred ones. For $x\in S$ and $m\in M$ let $x^{-1}(m)$ be the position of $m$ in $x$. Define the "score"
$$\langle x,z\rangle=\sum_{m\in M}x^{-1}(m)\,z^{-1}(m).$$
For each $x\in P$ let $A(x)$ be the set of $z\in S$ for which $x$ maximises $\langle\cdot,z\rangle$ over $P$. Every $z\in S$ lies in some $A(x)$ (take a maximiser over the finite nonempty set $P$), so
$$n!=|S|\le\sum_{x\in P}|A(x)| .$$
It therefore suffices to show $|A(x)|\le n!/k!$ for each $x\in P$; then $|P|\ge k!$.

Fix $x\in P$, its indices $i_1<\dots<i_k$ from the statement, and put $m_j=x_{i_j}$. Let $z\in A(x)$ and $1\le s<k$. Swapping $m_s$ and $m_{s+1}$ in $x$ gives a preferred $y$, which differs from $x$ only in the positions of $m_s,m_{s+1}$. Since $\langle x,z\rangle\ge\langle y,z\rangle$,
$$i_s\,z^{-1}(m_s)+i_{s+1}\,z^{-1}(m_{s+1})\ \ge\ i_{s+1}\,z^{-1}(m_s)+i_s\,z^{-1}(m_{s+1}),$$
i.e. $(i_{s+1}-i_s)\big(z^{-1}(m_{s+1})-z^{-1}(m_s)\big)\ge0$. As $i_{s+1}>i_s$ and positions are distinct, $z^{-1}(m_{s+1})>z^{-1}(m_s)$.

So in every $z\in A(x)$ the fruits $m_1,m_2,\dots,m_k$ appear in this order. Among all $n!$ permutations, the $k$ given elements appear in each of the $k!$ possible relative orders equally often, so exactly $n!/k!$ permutations have them in the order $m_1,\dots,m_k$. Hence $|A(x)|\le n!/k!$, and Ivan prefers at least $k!$ permutations. ∎

prompt:
Ivan writes the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ on the board. Then he performs the following operation on the matrix several times:

* he chooses a row or a column of the matrix, and
* he multiplies or divides the chosen row or column entry-wise by the other row or column, respectively.

Can Ivan end up with the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ after finitely many steps?
answer: No

solutions.title: Take logarithms: the determinant is invariant
solutions.body:
**Answer: no.**

All entries stay positive (we only multiply and divide positive numbers). For a matrix $X=(x_{ij})$ with positive entries let $L(X)=(\log_2x_{ij})$. Multiplying (dividing) a row entry-wise by the other row turns into adding (subtracting) that row to the other row of $L(X)$; the same holds for columns. These elementary operations do not change the determinant, so $\det L(X)$ is invariant.

For the starting matrix,
$$\det L\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&\log_23\\1&2\end{pmatrix}=2-\log_23>0,$$
while for the target
$$\det L\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\2&3\end{pmatrix}=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&\log_23\end{pmatrix}=\log_23-2<0 .$$
The values differ, so Ivan cannot reach the second matrix. ∎

solutions.title: Track exponents of $2$ and $3$
solutions.body:
Every entry that ever appears is of the form $2^a3^b$ with integers $a,b$ (true initially and preserved by multiplication/division). Record a matrix by two integer matrices $E$ (exponents of $2$) and $F$ (exponents of $3$), and consider the polynomial
$$\Delta(t)=\det(E+tF).$$
An operation adds or subtracts one row (column) of $E$ to the other and does the same to $F$, hence to $E+tF$; such operations preserve the determinant, so $\Delta(t)$ is invariant.

Initially $E=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, $F=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\Delta(t)=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\1&2\end{pmatrix}=2-t$. For the target, $E=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $\Delta(t)=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&t\end{pmatrix}=t-2$. Since $2-t\ne t-2$, the target is unreachable.

**Answer: no.** ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be the set of all continuous functions $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$, differentiable on $(0,1)$, with the property that $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=1$. Determine all $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ such that for every $f\in V$, there exists some $\xi\in(0,1)$ such that
$$f(\xi)+\alpha=f'(\xi).$$

solutions.title: A special function and Rolle's theorem
solutions.body:
**Answer: $\alpha=\dfrac1{e-1}$ only.**
